descriptors.title: Australia's system of government
descriptors.description: the key features of Australia's system of government, including democracy, the Australian Constitution, responsible government and federalism
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the key institutions of Australia's system of government, that it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies (AC9HS6K06). They understand the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government (AC9HS6K07) and the events leading to Federation and the Constitution (AC9HS6K01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the key features of Australia's system of government, including democracy, the Australian Constitution, responsible government and federalism.

nodes.label: The Australian Constitution as foundation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role of the Australian Constitution as the foundational legal document establishing the structure and powers of Australia's national government.
criteria: Identify the Australian Constitution as the foundational document establishing the structure and powers of the national government
Describe at least two key institutions or roles established by the Australian Constitution
nodes.hinge_reason: If students don't grasp the Constitution as the foundational source of governmental authority, subsequent nodes about responsible government, federalism, and separation of powers lack the grounding needed — students will treat institutions as arbitrary structures rather than constitutionally-rooted arrangements.

width.minimum: Describe what the Australian Constitution is, when it came into effect, and its central purpose of establishing the framework of government.
width.typical: Explain the origins of the Constitution, its role in establishing the Commonwealth Parliament (Senate and House of Representatives), the Governor-General, and the division between constitutional and non-constitutional powers.
wider: Investigate the 1901 federation debates and the key compromises made in drafting the Constitution, including the role of the Senate in representing smaller colonies
Explore how the Constitution can be changed through a double majority referendum, and examine examples of successful and failed referendum attempts
Compare Australia's constitutional model with the US written constitution and the UK's uncodified constitutional tradition

modes.reason: The Constitution's role as a constraint on government power is a genuinely difficult conceptual move — invest in unpacking why a written document has this authority and what happens when governments exceed constitutional limits.
Examining the historical context of Federation and comparisons with other constitutional models helps students understand why this particular constitutional structure was chosen.

nodes.label: Representative and responsible government
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the principles of representative and responsible government, including the roles of the Governor-General, Parliament, Prime Minister and Cabinet, and the relationship between the executive and the legislature.
criteria: Explain how the Prime Minister and Cabinet are drawn from and accountable to Parliament
Describe the role of at least two institutions established by the Constitution (e.g. Governor-General, Senate, House of Representatives)
nodes.hinge_reason: The accountability relationship between the executive and legislature is central to understanding how responsible government works and why it differs from other democratic models. Thin understanding here means students misread how political power actually operates in Australia.

width.minimum: Explain that in a representative democracy citizens elect members of parliament, and that the executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature.
width.typical: Explain the roles of the Governor-General, the Senate, the House of Representatives, the Prime Minister, Cabinet, and the Opposition; describe how the executive is accountable to Parliament and how this distinguishes responsible government from other systems.
wider: Investigate a specific constitutional crisis (such as 1975) to examine how the principles of responsible government can be tested in practice
Compare Australia's responsible government model with a presidential system (e.g. USA) where the executive is separate from the legislature
Explore how question time, motions of no confidence, and Senate estimates function as mechanisms of parliamentary accountability

modes.reason: The concept of the executive being drawn from and accountable to the legislature is genuinely counter-intuitive for students — invest in the logical chain: election → parliament → government formation → accountability.
Examining concrete accountability mechanisms (question time, votes of no confidence) and historical examples helps students understand how the principle operates in practice.

nodes.label: Democratic principles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain key democratic concepts including popular sovereignty, representation, accountability, and the partial separation of powers in Australia's system.
criteria: Define popular sovereignty and explain its role in legitimising Australia's system of government
Explain what is meant by a 'partial separation of powers' in the Australian context

width.minimum: Explain popular sovereignty (that government authority derives from the people) and representation (that citizens elect members to act on their behalf) as foundations of Australian democracy.
width.typical: Explain popular sovereignty, representation, accountability, and Australia's partial separation of powers; describe how the legislative branch is elected by the people and from which the executive branch is drawn.
wider: Explore how the concept of popular sovereignty developed historically, from Magna Carta through Enlightenment thought to colonial self-government
Compare Australia's partial separation of powers with the United States' fuller separation to understand the different approaches to preventing concentration of power
Investigate how accountability mechanisms (elections, free press, independent judiciary) work together to operationalise democratic principles

modes.reason: The partial separation of powers is a nuanced concept — students need a clear reasoning scaffold to understand why Australia's system blends rather than separates executive and legislative functions.

nodes.label: Federalism and division of powers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain Australia as a federation with a constitutional division of powers and responsibilities between Commonwealth and state/territory governments.
criteria: Identify Australia as a federation and explain what this means for the distribution of governmental powers
Give examples of responsibilities held by the Commonwealth government and by state/territory governments

width.minimum: Identify that Australia is a federation in which the Constitution divides powers between the Commonwealth and state/territory governments, with examples of each.
width.typical: Explain the division of powers between Commonwealth and state/territory governments (exclusive, concurrent, and residual powers); describe examples of government responsibilities at each level and why federation was an appropriate structure for Australia.
wider: Investigate a contemporary policy area (e.g. health, education, water management) where Commonwealth and state responsibilities overlap and examine how intergovernmental relations manage these tensions
Explore High Court cases (such as Engineers' Case) that have shifted the balance of power between Commonwealth and states over time
Compare Australian federalism with another federation (e.g. Canada, Germany) to examine how different federal structures respond to the same challenge of distributing power

modes.reason: Federalism becomes meaningful when students see it operating in real policy domains — examining concurrent powers in a live policy area (health, education) is more effective than abstract descriptions of power categories.

nodes.label: Westminster and Washington influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the origins of Australia's system of government by identifying the aspects drawn from Westminster (British) and Washington (US) systems in the overall federation model.
criteria: Identify at least two features of Australia's system of government derived from the Westminster tradition and two from the US federal model
Explain why Australia's founders chose to combine features from both systems

width.minimum: Identify the main features Australia inherited from the Westminster system (responsible government, constitutional monarchy) and from the US federal model (Senate with equal state representation, written constitution).
width.typical: Explain how Australia's system of government synthesises Westminster responsible government with a federal structure inspired by the US model; describe why this hybrid arrangement was chosen and what problems it was designed to solve.
wider: Investigate how the founders of Australian federation deliberately chose to combine elements from both systems and what compromises and debates this involved
Compare how the Westminster and Washington systems handle the relationship between the executive and legislative branches, and identify which elements Australia adopted from each
Explore how Australia's model has evolved since Federation and whether it still reflects its Westminster/Washington origins

modes.reason: This node brings together the Westminster model (responsible government, parliament) and the federal structure (written constitution, Senate) established in earlier nodes — it is the synthesis point where the hybrid origins become explicit.

descriptors.title: Characteristics of Australia's democracy
descriptors.description: the characteristics of Australia's democracy, including freedom of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement
descriptors.knowledge: Students know key values and beliefs of Western democracies (AC9HS6K06) and can identify roles and responsibilities of different levels of government (AC9HS6K07). They understand that Australia's government emerged from Federation and is grounded in constitutional arrangements (AC9HS6K01, AC9HC7K01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the characteristics of Australia's democracy, including democratic freedoms and how they support active participation, and identify limits on these freedoms.

nodes.label: Democratic freedoms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the key democratic freedoms in Australia — freedom of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement — and their role in enabling democratic participation.
criteria: Name the five democratic freedoms and explain the role of each in enabling participation in democracy
Give a concrete example of how one freedom supports active civic participation
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the five freedoms as a connected set is foundational — without clarity on what each freedom is and why it matters, subsequent nodes about limits on freedoms and active citizenship have no base. Students who treat freedoms as a list to memorise rather than as principles will not be able to reason about why limits exist.

width.minimum: Name the five key democratic freedoms and explain in general terms why each is important for people to participate in democracy.
width.typical: Explain each of the five democratic freedoms (speech, association, assembly, religion, movement) and give examples of how each supports active participation in Australia's democracy — including voting, protest, community organising, and religious practice.
wider: Compare the protection of democratic freedoms in Australia with a country that has a formal bill of rights, exploring what difference constitutional protection makes
Examine historical cases in Australia where democratic freedoms have been contested or restricted, such as wartime censorship or Cold War anti-communist legislation
Investigate how Australia's democratic freedoms compare with international human rights frameworks such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights

modes.reason: Students need a clear repertoire of the five freedoms with concrete examples of each — building this range is the foundation before reasoning about limits and participation.

nodes.label: Limits on democratic freedoms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that democratic freedoms are not absolute and can be limited 'within the bounds of law', and identify reasons why such limits exist.
criteria: Explain that democratic freedoms can be limited by law and identify at least one reason why such limits exist
Give an example of a legal limit on a democratic freedom and explain the purpose of that limit

width.minimum: Explain that democratic freedoms can be limited by law and give at least one example of a legal limit on a freedom and the reason for it (e.g. defamation law limits freedom of speech to protect individuals).
width.typical: Explain that democratic freedoms are subject to legal limits and identify examples of how the law limits freedoms of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement; explain the reasons for such limits (e.g. protecting others' rights, national security, public order).
wider: Investigate a specific legal case where freedom of speech was tested in Australian courts, examining how courts balance competing rights
Explore how the limits on democratic freedoms in Australia compare with formal constitutional protections in other countries

Examine First Nations Australians' experience of legally enforced limits on freedoms (e.g. historical restrictions on movement under Protection Acts) and how this shapes understanding of democratic freedom

modes.reason: The concept of freedoms that are simultaneously protected and limited requires careful reasoning — students need to understand why a freedom can be both real and bounded, and what makes a legal limit legitimate rather than arbitrary.

nodes.label: Ways of participating in democracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and compare different ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy, including formal and informal mechanisms.
criteria: Identify at least three ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy
Explain why some forms of participation might be more effective than others for a given civic goal

width.minimum: Identify at least three ways citizens can participate in Australia's democracy (e.g. voting, petitioning, joining community organisations) and explain what each involves.
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of formal and informal participation mechanisms — voting, standing for parliament, contributing to parliamentary inquiries, petitions, social media campaigns, protest, volunteering, and community organisations — and compare their effectiveness for different purposes.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of different participation methods for specific civic goals (e.g. changing a law vs raising awareness vs influencing local decisions)
Investigate how digital tools and social media have changed the landscape of civic participation, including both new opportunities and risks
Examine examples of participation by young people and First Nations Australians, exploring what barriers and enablers exist for different groups

modes.reason: Students benefit from encountering the full range of participation forms — not just voting — to understand democracy as an ongoing practice rather than a periodic event.

nodes.label: Formal and active citizenship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between formal citizenship (legal status) and active citizenship (engaged participation), and identify who has been included and excluded from citizenship rights in Australia, particularly in relation to First Nations Australians.
criteria: Distinguish formal citizenship from active citizenship and explain what each involves
Identify that not all people in Australia have historically had equal access to citizenship rights, with reference to First Nations Australians

width.minimum: Distinguish formal citizenship (legal membership of the nation, with associated rights) from active citizenship (engaged participation in civic life); identify that not all people in Australia have always had equal citizenship rights.
width.typical: Explain the attributes of formal and active citizenship; identify how First Nations Australians and other groups have been excluded from full citizenship rights and freedoms historically, and examine examples of First Nations Australians' active citizenship and advocacy (e.g. Neville Bonner, Adam Goodes, Noel Pearson, Ellie Gaffney).
wider: Investigate the 1967 referendum and the campaign leading to it as a case of active citizenship driving constitutional change

Examine the contributions of specific First Nations Australian citizens (Neville Bonner, Adam Goodes, Noel Pearson, Murundoo Yanner, Charles Mene, Ellie Gaffney, Evelyn Scott, Pat O'Shane) and the significance of their advocacy
Explore what it means to 'become' an Australian citizen through naturalisation, and what rights and responsibilities this confers

modes.reason: The exclusion of First Nations Australians from citizenship rights is not background information — it is central to understanding what Australian democracy has meant in practice. These cases must be substantively engaged with, not mentioned in passing.

descriptors.title: The Australian legal system
descriptors.description: the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Australian Constitution, the rule of law and the court system
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that Australia's Constitution established the framework of government (AC9HC7K01). They know about democratic values including fairness and equality from primary HASS (AC9HS6K06). This is the first systematic treatment of Australia's legal system as a distinct institution.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Constitution, the rule of law, principles of justice and the court hierarchy.

nodes.label: Origins of Australia's legal system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the origins of Australia's legal system, including British common law, the Magna Carta, and the establishment of an independent judiciary.
criteria: Identify that Australia's legal system is based on British common law
Explain the key principle that no person is above the law and trace its origins to the Magna Carta
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of common law and its basis in precedent is foundational for understanding how Australian law develops and why court hierarchy matters. Students who don't grasp the origin story will treat the court system as arbitrary bureaucracy rather than a principled institution.

width.minimum: Identify that Australia's legal system is based on British common law and explain the key principle inherited from the Magna Carta that no person is above the law.
width.typical: Explain the origins of Australia's legal system in British common law and the Magna Carta; describe the role of an independent judiciary in applying the law impartially; identify the federal and state/territory court hierarchies.
wider: Investigate the historical significance of the Magna Carta (1215) and trace how its principles of limiting government power and protecting individual rights developed into modern Australian law
Explore how Australian common law has developed differently from UK law since 1901, including landmark cases that changed Australian law
Examine the concept of legal precedent (stare decisis) and how decisions made in higher courts bind lower courts

modes.reason: The idea that law can be 'made' through judicial decisions (common law) rather than only through legislation is genuinely novel — invest in the reasoning scaffold that shows how precedent accumulates into binding legal principles.

nodes.label: Rule of law and principles of justice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the rule of law and the principles of justice, fairness, equality, presumption of innocence, burden of proof, and the right to a fair trial.
criteria: Explain the rule of law and what it means for how law is applied in Australia
Identify at least two principles of a fair legal system (e.g. presumption of innocence, burden of proof) and explain why each matters
nodes.hinge_reason: The rule of law and fair trial principles are the conceptual core of the legal system. Without understanding these, students cannot assess whether a legal system is working as intended or evaluate proposed reforms. The concepts in K04 and K05 (social cohesion, democratic values) rely on students grasping why impartial law matters.

width.minimum: Explain the rule of law (that everyone is subject to the same law, applied equally) and identify at least two principles of a fair legal system (e.g. presumption of innocence, right to a fair trial).
width.typical: Explain the rule of law and its relationship to democratic principles; describe the principles of justice, fairness, equality, presumption of innocence, burden of proof, and the right to a fair trial and legal representation; make connections between these principles and democratic values.
wider: Investigate examples where the rule of law has been challenged in Australia, such as cases involving the legality of government actions, and examine how the courts resolved them
Examine how the principle of equal access to justice operates in practice through legal aid, community legal centres, and self-represented litigants
Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have experienced the Australian legal system, including historical inequalities in the application of law

modes.reason: The rule of law needs careful unpacking — students need to understand why equal application of law is a principled achievement, not a given, and what happens when it fails.

First Nations Australians' historical experience of unequal application of law provides concrete context for understanding why rule of law principles matter and what is at stake when they are not upheld.

nodes.label: Court hierarchy and fair trial
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe Australia's court hierarchy (federal and state/territory) and explain the elements of a fair trial, including the roles of witnesses, jurors, legal representation, and due process.
criteria: Identify at least three levels of the Australian court hierarchy and describe the role of each
Explain two elements of a fair trial and why each is important to a just legal system

width.minimum: Identify that Australia has a hierarchy of courts (magistrates, district/county, supreme, and federal) and explain at least two elements of a fair trial (e.g. legal representation, role of jurors).
width.typical: Describe the federal and state/territory court hierarchies; explain the elements of a fair trial including the roles of citizens as witnesses and jurors, legal representation, due process, and the significance of an independent judiciary.
wider: Investigate how a case moves through the court hierarchy (from lower to higher courts on appeal) using a real or hypothetical case
Explore how legal aid and community legal services provide access to justice for people who cannot afford legal representation
Examine the role of the jury system in Australian democracy — why citizens are asked to make legal judgments and what obligations this creates

modes.reason: Tracing a case through the court hierarchy using a concrete example is more effective than describing the hierarchy in the abstract — the procedural logic becomes clearer when students see it in motion.

nodes.label: Legal system and democratic principles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the connections between a fair and just legal system and democratic principles, and understand how access to justice is supported in Australia.
criteria: Explain at least one connection between a fair legal system and democratic principles
Describe how citizens can access legal representation and justice in Australia

width.minimum: Explain one connection between the rule of law and democratic principles (e.g. legal equality supports democratic equality) and identify that legal aid exists to support access to justice.
width.typical: Explain how a fair and just legal system supports democracy by enforcing rights, constraining government power, and providing mechanisms for resolving disputes; describe how Australians can access justice including through legal aid and legal representation.
wider: Investigate a reform to the Australian legal system that aimed to improve access to justice or equality before the law, and evaluate whether it achieved its goals
Explore how the legal system interacts with democratic rights — for example, how the right to protest is protected and how courts have interpreted free speech cases
Compare access to justice across different groups in Australia (e.g. by socioeconomic status, location, cultural background) and identify systemic barriers

modes.reason: This node synthesises the constitutional foundation, rule of law, and court system into a coherent picture of how the legal system serves democratic values — it is the point where the building blocks connect.

descriptors.title: Secular democracy and pluralist society
descriptors.description: how Australia's secular democracy and pluralist, multi-faith society draws upon diverse cultural origins, including Christian and Western heritage, distinct First Nations Australian histories and cultures, and migrant communities
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand Australia's system of government and democratic freedoms (AC9HC7K01, AC9HC7K02). From primary HASS they know about migration and Australian society (AC9HS6K03) and diversity in communities. This descriptor extends that to the concept of secular democracy and the religious and cultural dimensions of Australian identity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how Australia's secular democracy and pluralist, multi-faith society draws upon diverse cultural origins including Christian and Western heritage, distinct First Nations histories and cultures, and migrant communities.

nodes.label: Key concepts: secular, pluralist, multi-faith
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define and explain the terms 'secular', 'pluralist', 'multi-faith', and 'diverse society', and discuss their relevance to contemporary Australia.
criteria: Define 'secular', 'pluralist', and 'multi-faith' and explain each term's relevance to Australia
Explain what it means for Australia to have a secular government within a multi-faith society
nodes.hinge_reason: Without clear understanding of what 'secular' means in Australian constitutional terms, students conflate secular government with irreligion or with hostility to religion — this leads to misreading subsequent nodes about Christian heritage and religious diversity in a pluralist society.

width.minimum: Define 'secular' (government separate from religion), 'multi-faith' (many religious traditions present), and 'pluralist' (diversity of beliefs and cultures respected), and give one example of each concept in Australian life.
width.typical: Define and discuss the terms 'secular', 'multi-faith', 'diverse society', 'culturally diverse', 'Christian heritage', 'Western heritage', and 'pluralist'; explain what it means for Australia to be simultaneously secular (in government) and multi-faith (in society).
wider: Investigate the distinction between a secular state (government does not favour any religion) and a secular society (religion plays little role in public life) — is Australia both, or just the former?
Compare Australia's secular constitutional arrangements with countries that have state religions, examining what difference this makes to religious freedom
Explore ABS census data on religious observance in Australia over recent decades to identify trends and discuss what they suggest about Australian society

modes.reason: The distinction between a secular state and a secular society is genuinely subtle — invest in unpacking why a secular government can coexist with high religious diversity and why this is seen as a democratic achievement.

nodes.label: Christian and Western heritage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the cultural and historical foundations of Australia's Christian heritage and their impact on Australia's political and legal systems.
criteria: Identify at least two ways Australia's Christian and Western heritage has shaped political or legal institutions
Acknowledge that the influence of Christian heritage has had varied impacts on different communities in Australia

width.minimum: Identify that Australia's political and legal systems have been significantly shaped by Christian and Western heritage, and give two examples of this influence (e.g. Sunday as a public holiday, parliamentary oath options, common law tradition).
width.typical: Explain the cultural and historical foundations of Australia's Christian and Western heritage; describe their influence on political institutions, legal principles, and social values; acknowledge the impacts this has had on First Nations Australian communities and other groups in Australian society.
wider: Investigate specific ways Christian traditions influenced the drafting of the Australian Constitution and early Commonwealth laws (e.g. s116 preventing religious tests for office)
Examine how Christian social teachings influenced social welfare legislation, labour rights, and public institutions in Australia's history
Explore how First Nations Australian communities experienced the imposition of Christian values and institutions through missions and government policies, and evaluate the mixed legacies

modes.reason: The impact of Christian heritage on First Nations communities through missions and government policies is a significant and contested dimension — engaging with this context is essential for an honest account, not optional enrichment.

nodes.label: First Nations Australian histories and cultures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the diversity of First Nations Australian communities and their distinct histories and cultures, including the distinctiveness of connections to Country/Place.
criteria: Describe the diversity of First Nations Australian communities and explain why they cannot be treated as a single homogeneous group
Explain the significance of connection to Country/Place in First Nations Australian cultures

width.minimum: Describe the diversity of First Nations Australian communities and explain the significance of connection to Country/Place as a distinctive feature of First Nations cultures.
width.typical: Explain the diversity of First Nations Australian communities, including the distinctiveness of their connections to Country/Place; explore the diversity of spiritualities among First Nations communities, from traditional spirituality to adoption of other religions; describe First Nations Australians as one of the foundational cultural origins of Australia's pluralist society.
wider: Investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian spiritualities and how these have interacted with introduced religions since colonisation
Examine how connection to Country/Place functions in First Nations cultures as a framework for relationships, responsibilities and law, and compare this with Western legal concepts of land ownership
Explore specific First Nations communities' histories and cultures to understand the diversity within the category 'First Nations Australians' — avoiding homogenisation

modes.reason: Avoiding homogenisation of First Nations cultures requires deliberate breadth — students need encounters with the diversity of communities, languages, spiritualities and connections to Country to resist treating 'First Nations Australians' as a monolithic category.

nodes.label: Migrant communities and contemporary diversity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how migrant communities contribute to Australia's pluralist, multi-faith society, and use data to identify trends in religious observance and cultural heritage.
criteria: Identify at least two religious or cultural traditions beyond Christianity that are part of contemporary Australian society
Explain how migrant communities contribute to Australia's pluralist, multi-faith identity

width.minimum: Identify that migrant communities are a significant source of cultural and religious diversity in Australia, and identify at least two religious traditions practised in contemporary Australia beyond Christianity.
width.typical: Explain how migrant communities have contributed to Australia's cultural and religious diversity; identify trends regarding religious observance and/or cultural heritage using ABS or similar data; describe religious traditions practised in contemporary Australia including Judaism, Buddhism, Islam and Hinduism.
wider: Analyse ABS census data on religious diversity across different postcode areas, age groups or decades to identify patterns and changes in Australia's religious landscape
Investigate the experiences of a specific migrant community in Australia — examining how they maintain cultural and religious identity while participating in Australian civic life
Explore how Australia's approach to multiculturalism has evolved as a policy framework for managing cultural and religious diversity

modes.reason: This node brings together the Christian/Western heritage, First Nations cultures, and migrant communities as the three foundational streams of Australia's pluralist society — it is the synthesis point where students see how Australia's multi-faith, diverse character emerged from multiple historical layers.

descriptors.title: Values, social cohesion and democracy
descriptors.description: how values based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity can support social cohesion and democracy within Australian society
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand Australia's democratic freedoms and the characteristics of active and formal citizenship (AC9HC7K02). They have explored Australia's pluralist, multi-faith society and diverse cultural origins (AC9HC7K04). This descriptor extends that to examine how shared values can hold a diverse society together.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how values based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity can support social cohesion and democracy, evaluating the extent to which these values are reflected in Australian society.

nodes.label: Australian values and their expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify Australian values including freedom, respect, fairness, equality, compassion, and a 'fair go', and explain how these values are expressed through customs, protocols, and civic life.
criteria: Identify at least four Australian civic values and explain what each means
Describe at least one way Australian values are expressed through public customs or protocols

width.minimum: Identify at least four Australian values (e.g. freedom, fairness, equality, a 'fair go') and describe one way each is expressed in Australian public or civic life.
width.typical: Identify a range of Australian values including patriotism, inclusion, civility, personal and collective responsibility, compassion, equality, justice, a 'fair go', and religious freedom; explain how these values are expressed through customs and protocols such as flag-raising ceremonies and the national anthem; investigate the history of changes to the national anthem.
wider: Investigate how the concept of a 'fair go' has been interpreted differently by different groups in Australian society, including debates about whether it is a lived reality or an aspiration
Explore how shared values can be expressed differently across cultural communities in Australia — examining how the same value manifests in different traditions
Compare Australian civic values with those articulated in national identity documents from other countries (e.g. the US Declaration of Independence, the French Republic's motto)

modes.reason: Students need to build a genuine repertoire of Australian civic values with concrete examples — this is the factual foundation before evaluating how well values are upheld.

nodes.label: Values and social cohesion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how shared values can promote social cohesion and reconciliation in Australia's diverse society, and evaluate the extent to which these values are reflected in Australian society.
criteria: Explain what social cohesion means and identify how shared values support it in a diverse society
Evaluate at least one area where Australian values are strongly reflected and one area where there is a gap between aspiration and reality
nodes.hinge_reason: The evaluation of whether values are actually reflected in society — not just stated — is the conceptual core of this descriptor. Students who only identify values without evaluating their application cannot meet the descriptor's command term ('can support') which implies a conditional, evaluative claim.

width.minimum: Explain what 'social cohesion' means and identify at least one way shared values (e.g. fairness, inclusion) support people from diverse backgrounds living together in Australian society.
width.typical: Explain how shared values support social cohesion in a diverse society; evaluate the extent to which values like freedom, respect, fairness and equality are genuinely reflected in Australian society, including examining where gaps between aspiration and reality exist; consider how these values can promote reconciliation.
wider: Evaluate the extent to which Australian values are reflected across different groups — examining evidence of inequality, discrimination or exclusion that challenges claims about shared values

Investigate how reconciliation between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians is understood as a values-driven process, and examine specific initiatives (e.g. Sorry Day, Reconciliation Action Plans)
Explore how migrants and refugees experience Australian values when arriving in Australia — what aspects of Australian civic life help or hinder their participation

modes.reason: Evaluating the gap between stated values and lived reality requires careful reasoning — students need a scaffold for assessing evidence of both alignment and failure, and for making conditional claims about what values 'can' (but do not always) achieve.

Reconciliation as a values-driven process offers rich context for exploring how social cohesion is actively built rather than passively assumed — examine specific initiatives alongside the ongoing gaps.

nodes.label: Religious and Christian traditions in Australian society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify Christian traditions and values that have influenced the development of Australian society, democracy and law, and identify the values and beliefs of other religions practised in contemporary Australia.
criteria: Identify at least two Christian traditions that have shaped Australian society or law
Name at least two other religions practised in contemporary Australia and describe one key value or belief of each

width.minimum: Identify at least two Christian traditions or values that have shaped Australian society, democracy or law, and name at least two other religions practised in contemporary Australia.
width.typical: Identify Christian traditions and values that have influenced Australian society, democracy and law (including impacts on First Nations communities and other groups); identify the values and beliefs of religions practised in contemporary Australia such as Judaism, Buddhism, Islam and Hinduism.
wider: Investigate the influence of Christian social teaching on Australian social policy areas such as healthcare, education and welfare, tracing connections to current institutions
Compare the core values and beliefs of two or more religions practised in Australia to identify areas of common ground and difference
Explore how religious diversity in Australia is managed through legal protections (freedom of religion) and social norms of tolerance, and examine cases where religious freedom has been contested

modes.reason: Comparative engagement with multiple religious traditions (not just naming them) helps students genuinely understand pluralism rather than just identifying diversity as a list.

nodes.label: Migrants, refugees and Australian values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why migrants and refugees choose to come to Australia, connecting this to the values and freedoms that characterise Australian society.
criteria: Identify at least two reasons why people choose to migrate to Australia and connect at least one to Australian democratic values
Explain how Australian values and freedoms are relevant to the decisions migrants and refugees make

width.minimum: Identify at least two reasons why people choose to migrate to or seek refuge in Australia, connecting at least one to Australian democratic values or freedoms.
width.typical: Investigate why migrants and refugees wish to come to Australia and become Australian citizens; explain how Australian values (freedom, safety, rule of law, opportunity) attract people from other countries; evaluate how the reality of life in Australia aligns with migrants' and refugees' expectations.
wider: Investigate the experiences of refugees from a specific country of origin, examining what they are seeking in Australia and how well Australia's values and systems meet those needs
Explore the citizenship process and what obligations and rights come with Australian citizenship, connecting this to the values underpinning citizenship
Examine debates in Australia about immigration and refugee policy, connecting these to values of fairness, compassion, and security to analyse competing value claims

modes.reason: This node integrates the earlier examination of Australian values with a perspective from outside — people choosing Australia connects the values to their lived attractiveness and tests whether values are genuinely reflected in Australian life.

descriptors.title: Developing inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems (AC9HS6S01). At Y7 the shift is from general HASS inquiry questions to discipline-specific civics questions grounded in understanding of political and legal systems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop focused questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues.

nodes.label: Characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions — those that are focused, investigable, and connected to genuine issues in political or legal systems.
criteria: Identify at least two characteristics of an effective civic inquiry question
Distinguish between a too-broad question and a focused, investigable question and explain the difference
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish productive from unproductive inquiry questions, the investigation phase (S02, S03) will be misdirected — either scope creep or investigation of trivially answerable questions. This is the phase-entry gate for civic inquiry work.

width.minimum: Distinguish between a too-broad question (e.g. 'What is democracy?') and a focused inquiry question (e.g. 'How does Australia's federal system divide powers?') and explain what makes the second more useful for investigation.
width.typical: Identify the characteristics of effective civic inquiry questions: focused scope, investigable with available sources, connected to real issues in political or legal systems; practise identifying which questions are well-scoped vs too broad or too narrow.
wider: Evaluate a set of example inquiry questions against quality criteria, ranking and justifying which would lead to the most productive investigations
Compare civic inquiry questions with scientific or historical inquiry questions to understand what disciplinary thinking looks like in each context
Develop criteria for assessing the quality of an inquiry question and apply them to evaluate questions generated by others

modes.reason: Understanding what makes an inquiry question 'good' is a meta-cognitive step — students need to reason about the question itself before they can use it as an investigation tool. Invest in the criteria explicitly.

nodes.label: Developing a key inquiry question
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a focused key inquiry question related to a specific political or legal system topic, and explain what the question is designed to investigate.
criteria: Develop a focused inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system
Explain what the question is designed to investigate and identify what sources would be useful

width.minimum: Develop one focused inquiry question related to Australia's political or legal system and explain what a student would need to investigate to answer it.
width.typical: Develop a key question for a specific investigation (e.g. 'What is the rule of law and how does it apply to Australia's legal system?' or 'How does Australia's federal system divide powers?'); explain the scope and purpose of the question; identify what kinds of sources would help answer it.
wider: Develop a sequence of sub-questions from a key inquiry question, mapping how they build toward a complete answer
Revise an inquiry question after initial research to sharpen its focus or correct a misunderstanding — practising question iteration
Generate inquiry questions from current media coverage of a civic issue, practising how contemporary events can sharpen investigation focus

modes.reason: Developing a good inquiry question requires iteration and practice — students who produce their first question rarely get it right. Allow time for revision and peer critique before committing to an investigation path.

nodes.label: Using current events to generate civic questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use current events to generate focused questions that apply to a wider civic investigation, connecting news events to the underlying political or legal concepts they illustrate.
criteria: Identify a current event related to a civic issue and develop a focused question connecting it to a broader civic concept
Explain what makes this question more useful for civic investigation than simply asking 'what happened'

width.minimum: Identify a current news event related to a civic issue and develop one question that connects the event to a broader political or legal concept.
width.typical: Use current events to generate questions that apply to a wider investigation; for example, derive a question about freedom of expression protections from a news story about misinformation; explain how the current event illustrates an underlying civic issue.
wider: Track a developing news story over several days and generate a sequence of questions that evolve as new information emerges, practising the dynamic nature of inquiry
Compare how the same current event generates different inquiry questions depending on whether the investigator is using a democratic, legal, or social cohesion lens
Investigate an international civic issue and develop questions that allow comparison with Australian systems — practising cross-contextual civic inquiry

modes.reason: Different current events surface different types of civic questions — using varied events (court decisions, election campaigns, government announcements, protest actions) builds the range of question types students can generate.

descriptors.title: Locating and organising information
descriptors.description: locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats (AC9HS6S02). The Y7 shift is to civics-specific source types (government websites, specialist reports, legislation) and a more deliberate approach to source selection and organisation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources relevant to political, legal and civic investigations.

nodes.label: Identifying and using civics-relevant sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the types of sources relevant to civic investigations (government websites, media, specialist reports, statistics) and explain why different source types are appropriate for different purposes.
criteria: Identify at least three source types relevant to civic investigations and explain what each provides
Match a given inquiry question to the most appropriate source type and explain the choice
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate source types for civic claims, their research (S02) and analysis (S03) will be built on poorly selected evidence. This is the source literacy gate for civic inquiry.

width.minimum: Identify at least three types of sources useful for civic investigations (e.g. government websites, news articles, specialist reports) and explain what kind of information each provides.
width.typical: Identify the range of source types relevant to civics — government websites, media reports, articles, graphs, charts, statistics, specialist reports from bodies like the Australian Law Reform Commission — and explain which source types are most appropriate for finding information about government systems, legal principles, cultural diversity, and civic issues.
wider: Evaluate the relative authority of different source types for civic claims — comparing a government website, a newspaper editorial, and a specialist report on the same issue
Investigate how to access official sources such as the Australian Law Reform Commission reports, parliamentary Hansard, and ABS data for civics research
Explore the difference between primary sources (legislation, Hansard, court decisions) and secondary sources (media, commentaries) in a civic research context

modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of civics-specific source types — not just 'Google it', but knowing when to look at Hansard, ABS, specialist commission reports, or government websites. Practise finding the right type for different question types.

nodes.label: Locating information using search strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use targeted search strategies including advanced search functions to locate relevant information for civic investigations.
criteria: Use at least one targeted search strategy beyond basic keywords to locate relevant civic information
Identify an appropriate online source for a given civic research question

width.minimum: Use a focused search query (including at least one search strategy beyond a basic keyword search) to locate information relevant to a civic question.
width.typical: Locate information using advanced search strategies including targeted criteria (e.g. allintext: searches, site: searches, date filters); use online sources effectively to find government websites, reports, statistics and media coverage relevant to civic investigations.
wider: Use multiple search strategies on the same question and compare the results to evaluate which strategy was most effective for finding relevant civic information
Practice locating primary sources directly (e.g. finding legislation on legislation.gov.au, Hansard on aph.gov.au) rather than relying on secondary reporting
Investigate how to evaluate the currency and authority of online sources — practising source evaluation alongside source location

modes.reason: Advanced search skills require practice — basic keyword searching is the default and students need repeated opportunities to use more targeted strategies before they become habitual.

nodes.label: Selecting and organising information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select information from multiple sources on the basis of similarity and relevance to the investigation topic, and organise it coherently for analysis.
criteria: Select information from at least two sources that is relevant to a civic inquiry question
Organise selected information so that similar ideas from different sources are grouped, not just listed by source

width.minimum: Select information from at least two different sources that is relevant to a civic inquiry question, and organise it so that similar ideas from different sources are grouped together.
width.typical: Select and organise information from different sources (media reports, online publications, government websites) on the basis of similarity and relevance; identify key findings from specialist sources such as Law Reform Commission reports; organise information in a format that supports analysis (e.g. comparison table, annotated notes, concept map).
wider: Develop a structured note-taking system that tracks which source each piece of information came from, supporting later citation and attribution
Practice organising conflicting information from different sources — identifying where sources agree and disagree rather than only looking for supporting evidence
Organise information from a civic investigation into a structure that anticipates an argument or explanation, moving from collection to analytical organisation

modes.reason: Organising information by similarity and relevance (rather than by source) is a cognitive step that many students skip — practise is needed to build the habit of synthesising rather than summarising.

descriptors.title: Analysing information and perspectives
descriptors.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate information to identify patterns, trends, and relationships (AC9HS6S03) and evaluate sources and perspectives (AC9HS6S04). The Y7 shift is to explicitly civic analytical work — identifying how perspectives on political and legal issues differ and why, and what challenges arise from this.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse information, data and ideas about civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges.

nodes.label: Identifying perspectives in civic sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the perspective expressed in a civic source — who produced it, what position it represents, and how this shapes the information it contains.
criteria: Identify the perspective represented by a civic source and explain how that perspective might influence the information it contains
Identify at least one perspective that might be absent from a given source
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying perspective is the prerequisite for explaining differences between perspectives — students who cannot see a source as a positioned view rather than neutral information cannot meaningfully compare perspectives or identify challenges.

width.minimum: Identify the source of a piece of civic information (e.g. government website, newspaper editorial, advocacy group report), describe whose perspective it represents, and explain how that perspective might shape the information.
width.typical: Examine online publications or media reports and identify the perspective each represents; explain how a government source, a civil society source, and a media source on the same issue might present the information differently; identify whose perspective might be absent from each source.
wider: Compare multiple sources on the same civic issue (e.g. court system reform) from different institutional perspectives — government, legal profession, advocacy group, media — to map the range of viewpoints
Investigate how the framing of a civic issue (e.g. which facts are emphasised, what language is used) reflects the perspective of the source
Explore how First Nations Australians' perspectives on civic issues (e.g. land rights, constitutional recognition) may differ from mainstream government or media coverage of those issues

modes.reason: The move from 'what does this source say' to 'whose perspective does this source represent and how does that shape it' is a genuine conceptual step — invest in this distinction explicitly before moving to comparison.

nodes.label: Comparing and explaining perspective differences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the perspectives of different sources on the same civic issue and explain why their views differ.
criteria: Compare the perspectives of two sources on the same civic issue and identify at least one point of agreement and one of disagreement
Explain at least one reason why the perspectives differ

width.minimum: Compare two sources with different perspectives on the same civic issue and explain at least one reason why their views differ.
width.typical: Compare perspectives from multiple sources on a civic issue (e.g. a Lowy Institute poll vs a government statement vs media coverage); explain what causes perspective differences (different values, interests, access to information, institutional roles); draw preliminary conclusions about the issue based on this comparison.
wider: Evaluate which perspective is better supported by evidence for a given civic claim, distinguishing between value-based disagreements and factual disagreements
Investigate a civic issue where perspectives have changed over time (e.g. public views on same-sex marriage, Indigenous rights) to understand how perspectives evolve
Analyse data from surveys or polls (e.g. Lowy Institute, ABS) and compare the findings with qualitative perspectives from media or advocacy sources

modes.reason: Using a range of civic issues for perspective comparison (not just one case study) builds transferability — students need to practise the comparison skill across different types of civic questions (legal, governmental, social cohesion).

nodes.label: Identifying potential challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify potential challenges arising from perspective differences in civic issues — including challenges for policy, governance, social cohesion, or legal application.
criteria: Identify at least one potential challenge arising from competing perspectives on a civic issue
Explain what makes the challenge difficult to resolve with reference to the perspectives involved

width.minimum: Identify at least one potential challenge arising from competing perspectives on a civic issue (e.g. how to balance freedom of speech with the right to be protected from harmful speech).
width.typical: Analyse a civic issue to identify potential challenges arising from competing perspectives; explain what makes the challenge difficult to resolve (e.g. competing values, different stakeholder interests, gaps in evidence); connect the challenge to the broader system (legal, democratic, social) it arises within.
wider: Evaluate the court system's effectiveness by comparing perspectives of those who have used it, legal professionals, and reform advocates — drawing conclusions about systemic challenges

Investigate a contemporary civic challenge (e.g. balancing security and civil liberties, managing political misinformation) where perspectives genuinely conflict and identify what would need to change for progress
Explore how challenges to civic participation — barriers faced by different groups — create systemic issues for democratic representation

modes.reason: Identifying challenges requires integrating perspective analysis with knowledge of civic systems — students apply what they know about the legal or democratic system to diagnose why a particular challenge is hard to resolve.

descriptors.title: Methods for civic participation
descriptors.description: explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation
descriptors.knowledge: Students have examined ways citizens can participate in democracy (AC9HC7K02) and can assess possible effects of actions and evaluate perspectives (AC9HS6S06). The Y7 capability shift is to explain the methods and strategies of civic participation — understanding how and why particular participation strategies are chosen, not just what they are.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the methods and strategies of civic participation, identifying how these contribute to democratic and just outcomes.

nodes.label: Features of civic participation methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the features of different civic participation methods — including their mechanisms, reach, and intended outcomes.
criteria: Identify at least three civic participation methods and describe the key features of each
Explain what makes a particular method appropriate for a specific type of civic goal
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear understanding of what each method involves and how it works, students cannot reason about which method is appropriate for a given civic goal — which is the core capability this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least three civic participation methods (e.g. petition, social media campaign, direct action) and describe the key features of each.
width.typical: Identify and explain the features of civic participation methods including social media campaigns, letters, petitions, participation in mediation or tribunals, and direct action; describe how each method works and what makes it appropriate for different civic goals.
wider: Investigate historical examples of each civic participation method (e.g. a successful petition campaign, a landmark tribunal case) to understand how the method works in practice
Compare civic participation methods available in Australia with those in a country with fewer democratic freedoms to appreciate the significance of participatory rights
Explore how digital tools have created new forms of civic participation (e.g. online petitions, social media campaigns) and evaluate how these differ from traditional methods

modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of participation methods with genuine knowledge of how each works — not just a list of names. Practise describing what each method involves before moving to strategic reasoning about selection.

nodes.label: Responsibilities of active citizenship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the core responsibilities of active citizenship and evaluate how citizens enacting democratic values contribute to a cohesive society.
criteria: Identify at least two responsibilities of active citizenship and explain how they support democratic life
Give an example of active citizenship contributing to social cohesion and explain the connection

width.minimum: Identify at least two responsibilities associated with active citizenship (e.g. staying informed, contributing to community, participating in democratic processes) and explain how they contribute to democratic life.
width.typical: Identify the core responsibilities of active citizenship; evaluate how the contributions of citizens who enact democratic values (e.g. through disability advocacy services, Landcare groups, community organisations) demonstrate active citizenship and contribute to social cohesion; connect individual action to broader democratic outcomes.
wider: Investigate a specific community organisation or advocacy group (e.g. Landcare, disability advocacy services) and evaluate the contribution it makes to both local community and democratic participation
Examine what is meant by 'civic responsibility' in different cultural contexts — are the responsibilities of citizenship understood differently across communities?
Explore First Nations Australian conceptions of responsibility to community and Country as a form of active citizenship that predates colonial democratic institutions

modes.reason: Examining diverse examples of active citizenship (disability advocacy, environmental action, First Nations community organisations) helps students understand that active citizenship takes many forms and is not limited to formal political participation.

nodes.label: Choosing participation strategies for civic goals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how participation methods and strategies are linked to specific civic goals, identifying why certain methods are chosen to achieve democratic and just outcomes.
criteria: Explain why a particular civic participation method would be chosen for a specific civic goal
Identify the connection between participation strategy and intended democratic or just outcome

width.minimum: Explain why a given civic participation method (e.g. a petition, a social media campaign, a direct action) would be chosen for a particular civic goal, identifying the connection between method and intended outcome.
width.typical: Identify and evaluate the methods and actions linked to active and informed citizenship; explain how citizens and groups choose methods to achieve democratic and just outcomes in local, national, regional and global contexts; connect participation strategy to civic purpose (e.g. raising awareness vs creating legal change vs applying community pressure).
wider: Investigate a real civic campaign (e.g. heritage building preservation, green space protection, environmental advocacy) and analyse the participation strategies used and why they were effective or ineffective
Compare the participation strategies chosen by two different groups seeking the same civic outcome — evaluating which strategies were more effective and why
Design a civic participation strategy for a hypothetical local issue, justifying the choice of methods against the civic goal and the available participation options

modes.reason: This node integrates the repertoire of methods (N1) and the understanding of civic responsibilities (N2) into strategic reasoning about participation — students connect what methods are available with why a particular method serves a particular goal.

descriptors.title: Creating civic descriptions, explanations and arguments
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present descriptions and explanations drawing on sources and using relevant terms and conventions (AC9HS6S07). The Y7 shift is to civics-specific communication — using discipline concepts and terms (rule of law, separation of powers, secular nation), referencing evidence, and developing argument as a distinct form.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence.

nodes.label: Using civics concepts and terms accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in descriptions and explanations, connecting terms to their meanings rather than using them superficially.
criteria: Use at least three civics concepts or terms correctly in a piece of writing about a civic topic
Demonstrate that terms are used to communicate genuine understanding (not superficially) by explaining what each term means in context
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate use of civics concepts is the foundation for creating arguments that reference evidence — students who misuse terms will produce descriptions and arguments that fail to communicate genuine civic understanding. This is the language precision gate for civic communication.

width.minimum: Use at least three civics concepts or terms correctly in a description or explanation (e.g. 'rule of law', 'separation of powers', 'secular nation', 'federalism'), demonstrating understanding of what each term means.
width.typical: Use appropriate civics concepts and terms (including 'rule of law', 'separation of powers', 'secular nation', 'responsible government', 'federalism', 'active citizenship') accurately in descriptions and explanations; demonstrate that terms are used to communicate genuine understanding rather than as decoration.
wider: Explain the same civic concept using both formal disciplinary language and accessible everyday language, practising the ability to code-switch between registers
Analyse a student or media example to identify where civics terms are used correctly vs incorrectly or superficially, developing evaluative judgement about term use
Build a personalised civics glossary that defines terms in own words with example sentences, supporting fluent use in writing

modes.reason: Accurate term use requires practice and feedback — students need to see their term use evaluated and corrected, not just to learn definitions. Invest in regular writing tasks that require terms to be used in context.

nodes.label: Developing evidence-referenced explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop explanations that use civics knowledge and research to present an authoritative position on an issue, referencing specific evidence.
criteria: Write an explanation that references at least one piece of specific evidence
Connect the evidence to the explanation — showing why the evidence supports the claim rather than just listing it

width.minimum: Write an explanation of a civic issue or system that references at least one piece of specific evidence (e.g. a law, a statistic, an example) to support the explanation.
width.typical: Develop explanations using civic and citizenship knowledge or research that present an authoritative position; reference specific evidence (laws, data, examples, cases); connect evidence to explanation rather than listing facts alongside claims.
wider: Develop an explanation that integrates evidence from multiple source types (e.g. legislation + statistical data + expert report) and explains how the evidence sources support each other
Evaluate an explanation written by someone else to identify where evidence is well-integrated and where claims are unsubstantiated
Revise an explanation after receiving feedback on evidence use — practising the iterative writing process

modes.reason: Connecting evidence to claims (not just including evidence alongside claims) is a writing skill that requires practice and iterative feedback — students need to write, receive feedback, and revise to develop this skill.

nodes.label: Constructing civic arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a civic argument — a structured claim with supporting evidence and reasoning — appropriate to the purpose and audience, using relevant concepts and terms.
criteria: Construct a structured civic argument with a clear claim, at least two supporting points, and referenced evidence
Use at least two civics concepts or terms accurately and present ideas appropriate to the intended audience

width.minimum: Write a short argument (claim + at least two supporting points + evidence) on a civic topic, using at least two relevant civics terms and presenting ideas appropriate to the audience.
width.typical: Develop civic arguments using appropriate terms and concepts; present ideas appropriate to purpose and audience (e.g. digital material promoting democratic participation, a written case for constitutional change); structure arguments with a clear position, supporting points, evidence, and coherent reasoning.
wider: Develop an argument for a simulated civic context (e.g. a submission to a parliamentary committee, a speech for a school community forum) and adapt tone and structure to that specific audience and purpose
Compare two arguments taking opposing positions on the same civic issue, evaluating which is better supported and identifying the weaknesses in each
Develop a multi-modal civic communication (e.g. digital presentation promoting participation in democracy) that integrates text, evidence, and visual elements

modes.reason: Argument construction integrates accurate term use (N1), evidence referencing (N2), and knowledge of civic systems — the argument is the performance that draws on all previous capabilities and knowledge nodes.

descriptors.title: Democratic participation
descriptors.description: how Australians are informed about and participate in democracy
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the key features of Australia's system of government including democracy, the Constitution, responsible government and federalism (AC9HC7K01), and the characteristics of Australia's democracy including freedoms of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement (AC9HC7K02). They can explain how values of freedom, respect, fairness and equality support social cohesion (AC9HC7K05). The gap this descriptor fills is the mechanisms by which citizens actually participate in and are informed about that democratic system — moving from structural knowledge to participatory knowledge.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how Australians are informed about and participate in democracy, including the range of participatory mechanisms, how those mechanisms have changed over time, and the role of media, interest groups and campaigns in shaping informed citizenship.

nodes.label: Forms of democratic participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the main formal and informal ways Australians participate in democracy, including voting, contacting representatives, joining political parties, standing as candidates, using lobby groups, and taking direct action.
criteria: Can distinguish at least three distinct forms of democratic participation and describe the purpose of each
Can give a concrete example of each form they describe
nodes.hinge_reason: If students conflate different forms of participation or cannot distinguish formal mechanisms (voting, candidacy) from informal ones (lobbying, direct action), subsequent nodes about how government is formed and how influence is exercised cannot be grounded. This conceptual foundation underpins the analysis of electoral strategies and media influence in later nodes.

width.minimum: Describe at least three distinct forms of democratic participation with an example of each.
width.typical: Describe the full range of formal and informal participatory mechanisms — voting, contacting elected representatives, joining parties, standing as candidates, lobby groups and direct action — explaining the purpose and context of each.
wider: Compare participatory mechanisms across different levels of government (local, state, federal) and how the opportunities available vary by level
Investigate digital and online forms of participation (e-petitions, social media campaigns, online consultations) and how these have expanded the participatory landscape
Examine how participatory mechanisms differ in Australia compared to another democratic country

modes.reason: Students need to build a working repertoire of participatory forms before analysing how they operate. Invest time ensuring all major forms are understood with concrete examples — not just voting.

nodes.label: Voting rights and the AEC
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how voting rights in Australian democracy have changed since Federation and describe the role of the Australian Electoral Commission as an independent electoral service.
criteria: Can explain at least one significant change to voting rights since Federation, identifying who was excluded before the change and what changed
Can describe the AEC's function and explain why electoral administration needs to be independent of government
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that democratic rights were not given all at once — and that independent electoral administration is a structural safeguard — is necessary for students to meaningfully analyse citizenship and participation debates later in this descriptor and in K06. A thin treatment produces students who treat democratic rights as natural and universal rather than historically contingent.

width.minimum: Explain one significant change to voting rights since Federation (e.g. women's suffrage, Indigenous enfranchisement) and state the key role of the AEC.
width.typical: Explain the progressive expansion of voting rights since Federation — including women's suffrage, the removal of property qualifications, and the enfranchisement of First Nations Australians in 1962 — and describe the AEC's role in administering elections independently of government.
wider: Investigate the significance of the 1967 referendum and the 1962 Commonwealth Electoral Act for First Nations Australians' political participation and what each did and did not change
Compare the AEC's role and independence with electoral authorities in another country to examine what features of electoral administration matter most for democratic integrity
Examine debates about compulsory voting in Australia — its history, rationale and ongoing contestation

modes.reason: The expansion of voting rights is a rich set of cases — women's suffrage, First Nations enfranchisement, compulsory voting. Widening across these cases prevents students from treating one change as representative of all change.

nodes.label: Young people and political influence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify issues of concern to young Australians and explain different ways young people seek to influence political processes.
criteria: Can name at least two current issues of concern to young Australians
Can describe at least one strategy young people use to influence political processes and explain how it works

width.minimum: Identify at least two issues of concern to young Australians and describe one way young people seek to influence political processes.
width.typical: Examine several current issues of concern to young Australians (e.g. climate change, cost of living, mental health, social justice) and investigate a range of strategies young people use to influence political processes — including petitions, social media campaigns, youth advisory bodies, protests and direct political engagement.
wider: Analyse a specific youth-led political campaign in Australia, evaluating which participatory strategies were used and what impact they had
Investigate formal youth participation mechanisms such as the Australian Youth Forum or Youth Parliament and what they can and cannot achieve
Compare how young people's political influence and voting age varies across democratic countries

modes.reason: Students relate to this node personally. Widening across multiple issues and multiple participatory strategies builds a more realistic picture of youth civic engagement — preventing reduction to a single issue or a single action type.

nodes.label: Case study: citizen participation in political campaigns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse a case study of citizen participation in a political campaign, identifying the participatory strategies used and evaluating their significance.
criteria: Can identify at least two participatory strategies used in their chosen case study
Can explain the significance of the case study in terms of democratic participation — what it demonstrates about how citizens can seek political change

width.minimum: Describe one case study of citizen participation in a political campaign, identifying at least two participatory strategies used.
