Develop a multi-component civic communication product on a contemporary issue — combining a factual description, an explanatory piece and a persuasive argument to serve different audience needs on the same issue

modes.reason: Persuasive civic argument is the integration point for all skills developed in S01–S05: inquiry questions shaped the research, source organisation and perspective analysis informed the evidence, and terminology fluency from earlier nodes provides the language. This is the full descriptor demand — coordinate all components in the argument creation.

descriptors.title: Constitution and democratic processes
descriptors.description: the role of the Australian Constitution in providing the basis for Australia's federal system of government and democratic processes, including institutions, and the process for constitutional change through a referendum
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how Australians are informed about and participate in democracy (AC9HC8K01), and the role of political parties and independent representatives including elections and formation of governments (AC9HC8K02). They have a working understanding of democratic participation but have not yet examined the constitutional foundations underpinning these processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the role of the Australian Constitution in establishing Australia's federal system of government and democratic institutions, and describe the process and challenges of constitutional change through referendum.

nodes.label: Purpose and origins of the Constitution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why the Australian Constitution was written and the key compromises involved in Federation.
criteria: Explains at least one reason the colonies needed to compromise to achieve Federation
Identifies the Constitution as the document that established the rules for federal government
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not understand that the Constitution is a foundational legal document that structures government authority, the subsequent nodes — on what the Constitution enables and how it can be changed — lack grounding. Students who think of the Constitution as a policy document rather than a structural legal framework misread all downstream content.

width.minimum: Explain that the Constitution sets out the rules for Australia's federal government and was written before Federation to allow the colonies to unite, including at least one compromise made by the founding fathers.
width.typical: Describe the aims of the founding fathers and the need for compromise in writing the Constitution; explain how the Constitution established the federal system by distributing powers between the Commonwealth and the states.
wider: Investigate specific compromises made at Federation conventions (e.g. equal Senate representation for smaller states, retention of state courts) and assess whose interests they served
Compare the Australian Constitution's origins with another federation (e.g. the United States or Canada) to examine different approaches to federal design
Explore how First Nations Australians were excluded from constitutional deliberations at Federation and the significance of that exclusion

modes.reason: The concept of a constitution as a structural legal document (not a policy or aspirational statement) requires explicit scaffolding. Students need to understand the distinction between a rule about rules and ordinary laws before they can reason about what the Constitution enables.

nodes.label: Federal system and distribution of powers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the Constitution distributes powers between the Commonwealth and the states, and identify the democratic institutions it establishes.
criteria: Names at least two areas of federal government responsibility and two of state government responsibility
Identifies two constitutional institutions and explains their role in democratic government

width.minimum: Identify that the Constitution divides responsibilities between federal and state governments, and name at least two institutions established by the Constitution (e.g. Parliament, the High Court).
width.typical: Describe the federal system as a division of powers between the Commonwealth and states; explain the role of key institutions established by the Constitution (Parliament, the executive, the High Court); identify examples of federal vs state responsibilities and how conflicts are resolved.
wider: Investigate a specific area of federal-state conflict (e.g. environmental law, education funding, health) and analyse how constitutional division of powers has shaped that conflict
Examine the concept of a constitutional monarchy and how it operates in practice alongside parliamentary democracy
Compare federal systems in Australia and another country to explore different ways of distributing powers

modes.reason: Students commonly understand the federal system in the abstract but struggle to apply it to specific policy areas. Using two or three concrete examples of divided responsibility (roads, hospitals, defence) builds the working understanding needed for later analysis.

nodes.label: Constitutional protection of democratic processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the Constitution upholds democratic institutions and processes, including protections and limitations.
criteria: Identifies at least one democratic process or institution established by the Constitution
Explains at least one limitation in the Constitution's protection of individual rights or democratic participation

width.minimum: Explain at least one way the Constitution protects democratic processes (e.g. requiring elections, protecting freedom of political communication implied by the Constitution).
width.typical: Investigate the extent to which the Constitution upholds democratic institutions and processes, including: a constitutional monarchy, a federal parliamentary system with elected legislatures, protection of states' rights, and limited explicit rights protections; identify both what the Constitution enables and what it does not guarantee.
wider: Compare the constitutional protection of rights in Australia with a country that has an explicit bill of rights (e.g. the USA or Canada) and assess the implications for individual rights
Examine a High Court case in which constitutional interpretation shaped democratic practice (e.g. the implied freedom of political communication cases)
Investigate debates about whether Australia needs a bill of rights and evaluate arguments on both sides

modes.reason: Students often conflate 'democratic' with 'fully rights-protective', missing the distinction between structural democratic processes (elections, parliament) and substantive rights protections. A structured comparison exercise helps students evaluate what the Constitution does and does not guarantee.

nodes.label: Referendum process and constitutional change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the process for changing the Australian Constitution through referendum and assess why it is difficult.
criteria: Describes the double majority requirement for a successful referendum
Explains at least one advantage and one disadvantage of requiring a referendum to change the Constitution
Names at least one successful or unsuccessful referendum and states its outcome
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the referendum mechanism is the integration point for the whole standard — students need to connect the Constitution's foundational status (Nodes 1–3) with the logic of why such a document is deliberately hard to change. Thin treatment leaves the referendum as a procedural trivia item rather than a meaningful democratic mechanism.

width.minimum: Describe the double majority requirement for a successful referendum and explain why the Constitution can only be changed this way.
width.typical: Describe the full referendum process including how it is initiated and decided, the role of the Australian Electoral Commission, and the double majority requirement; explain the advantages and disadvantages of requiring a referendum for constitutional change; discuss examples of successful and unsuccessful referenda.
wider: Assess the effectiveness of constitutional change through referendum by examining both the successful 1967 referendum (Aboriginals) and the unsuccessful 1999 republic referendum, comparing the conditions that led to each outcome
Investigate why no referendum has succeeded since 1977 and evaluate whether the referendum threshold is an appropriate safeguard or barrier to democratic reform
Examine current debate about an Indigenous Voice to Parliament and consider what constitutional change would require

modes.reason: Working through specific referendum cases (successful and unsuccessful) makes the double majority requirement concrete and allows students to analyse what conditions lead to constitutional change. This is where the procedural knowledge becomes evaluative reasoning.

descriptors.title: Legislative policy processes
descriptors.description: the legislative processes through which federal government policy is shaped, developed and implemented
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the role of political parties and independent representatives in Australian democracy including elections and formation of governments (AC9HC8K02), and how statutory law is made through parliaments (AC9HC8K03). They understand the basic passage of a bill into law but have not examined the upstream policy process — how government decisions move from idea to legislation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the legislative processes through which federal government policy is shaped, developed and implemented, including the influences on policy formulation.

nodes.label: Federal responsibilities and policy scope
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the areas of federal government responsibility that define the scope of federal policy-making.
criteria: Names at least two policy areas that are federal government responsibility
Explains why those areas fall under Commonwealth rather than state responsibility
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding which level of government has responsibility for a policy area, students cannot meaningfully trace how federal policy is developed — they may apply federal policy processes to state policy areas or vice versa throughout the rest of the sequence.

width.minimum: Identify at least two areas of federal government responsibility as outlined in the Constitution and explain why these areas fall under federal rather than state jurisdiction.
width.typical: Locate areas of federal government responsibility as outlined in the Constitution; explain why federal policy operates in these areas; identify how conflicts over federal/state/territory responsibilities are resolved (e.g. inconsistency doctrine, referral of powers).
wider: Investigate a contemporary area of federal-state responsibility tension (e.g. natural disaster funding, public hospital funding) and analyse how the Constitution shapes who can act
Examine cases where states have referred powers to the Commonwealth and evaluate the implications for federal policy scope

modes.reason: Students often default to thinking 'the government' makes all policy without distinguishing federal from state responsibility. A structured exercise mapping policy areas to jurisdictions anchors the subsequent process tracing.

nodes.label: From idea to enacted legislation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the sequential stages through which a policy idea becomes enacted federal legislation.
criteria: Lists at least three stages in the process of a bill becoming law
Explains the role of at least one stage in shaping the final legislation

width.minimum: Chart the main stages of federal policy development from initial idea through to enacted legislation, naming at least three distinct stages.
width.typical: Chart the full process of policy development from initial idea to enacted legislation, including policy development, Cabinet consideration, drafting of a bill, passage through both Houses of Parliament, and Royal Assent; explain the role of each stage.
wider: Trace a specific piece of recent federal legislation (e.g. climate policy, workplace relations) through each stage, identifying where delays or changes occurred
Compare the legislative process in Australia's bicameral parliament with a unicameral state parliament to analyse how the Senate shapes federal legislation
Examine the role of Senate committees in shaping legislation and evaluate their contribution to democratic accountability

modes.reason: Students benefit from charting multiple examples of legislation through the process to distinguish the typical path from cases where the process is contested or drawn out. A single example risks being treated as the only pattern.

nodes.label: Influences on policy formulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse multiple influences on how federal policy is formulated and implemented.
criteria: Names at least two types of influence on policy formulation
Uses a specific federal policy to illustrate how at least one influence shaped the policy's development or implementation

width.minimum: Identify at least two different types of influences on federal policy formulation (e.g. political parties, interest groups, citizens) using a specific federal policy as an example.
width.typical: Use a specific federal policy to understand and analyse the range of influences on policy formulation and implementation, including: political parties, interest groups, citizens and public opinion, international influences, and the public service; explain how these influences interact and sometimes conflict.
wider: Investigate a policy area where international obligations (e.g. UN conventions, trade agreements) have shaped domestic federal legislation and evaluate the extent of that influence
Analyse the role of media campaigns or public advocacy in shifting federal policy on a contemporary issue

Compare the relative influence of different stakeholders (industry lobby vs community groups vs public service) in a specific policy case and assess whose interests were most reflected in the final legislation

modes.reason: Analysing influences on policy formulation becomes meaningful only when applied to a specific, concrete policy case. Using two different policy examples (e.g. one with strong industry influence, one with significant community pressure) helps students see that the influence mix varies by case.

descriptors.title: Court jurisdictions and tribunals
descriptors.description: the key features and jurisdictions of Australia's court system, and the operations of courts and tribunals
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the characteristics of laws and how they are made through parliaments and courts (AC9HC8K03), and the types of law in Australia including criminal and civil law and First Nations customary law (AC9HC8K04). They understand law is made through two mechanisms but have not yet examined how the court hierarchy is structured or how different courts exercise their jurisdiction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the key features and jurisdictions of Australia's court system, describe the operations of courts and tribunals, and explain how court judgements contribute to the development of law.

nodes.label: Court hierarchy and jurisdiction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structure of Australia's court hierarchy and explain what jurisdiction means in this context.
criteria: Names at least three levels of the court hierarchy in order
Explains what jurisdiction means and gives an example of a matter each court level can hear
nodes.hinge_reason: If students do not understand the concept of jurisdiction — that different courts have authority over different types and scales of matters — they cannot make sense of Node 2's civil/criminal distinction or Node 3's explanation of how judgements create precedent. Students who treat all courts as interchangeable cannot trace how matters progress through the system.

width.minimum: Identify the main levels of the Australian court hierarchy (Magistrates/Local Court, District/County Court, Supreme Court, High Court) and explain that each court's jurisdiction defines the matters it can hear.
width.typical: Create or interpret a visual representation of the Australian court hierarchy; explain what each court's jurisdiction covers (original and appellate); describe where most criminal and civil matters begin and how matters move up the hierarchy on appeal.
wider: Compare the structure and jurisdiction of courts in two Australian states and identify how federal and state court systems interact
Investigate the role of specialist courts and tribunals (e.g. Family Court, Administrative Tribunals, NCAT, VCAT) and explain why these exist alongside the general court hierarchy
Examine how the High Court's jurisdiction to hear constitutional challenges distinguishes it from all other courts in the hierarchy

modes.reason: The concept of jurisdiction is abstract; students benefit from a structured exercise mapping specific types of cases (minor traffic infringement, serious criminal trial, constitutional challenge) to the court that would hear them. This makes jurisdiction operational rather than definitional.

nodes.label: Civil and criminal law in practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use sample cases to explain the differences between civil and criminal law and how courts apply each.
criteria: Correctly classifies at least one sample case as civil or criminal and explains the reasoning
Identifies a difference in who initiates a civil case versus a criminal case

width.minimum: Use at least one sample case to explain the difference between a civil dispute and a criminal matter, including who brings the case and what the court can order.
width.typical: Use sample cases to investigate the differences between civil and criminal law — including who initiates action, burden of proof, and available remedies or penalties; explain how courts apply and interpret criminal laws and resolve civil disputes; distinguish between the roles of courts and tribunals.
wider: Investigate a specific civil case (e.g. a tort or contract dispute) and a specific criminal case and compare the process, parties, standards of proof and outcomes
Examine how the same event (e.g. assault, negligence) can give rise to both civil and criminal proceedings simultaneously, and evaluate the implications
Explore how tribunals differ from courts in resolving civil disputes and assess advantages and limitations of each pathway

modes.reason: The civil/criminal distinction is easier to apply than to define in the abstract. Using two or three contrasting sample cases (one clearly civil, one clearly criminal, one ambiguous) helps students build flexible understanding rather than pattern-matching on surface features.

nodes.label: Precedent and the development of law
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how court judgements impact on the development of law through statutory interpretation and the creation of precedent.
criteria: Explains what a legal precedent is and why courts follow them
Uses the Mabo Case (or equivalent) to illustrate how a court judgement can develop the law beyond statute

width.minimum: Explain that courts interpret laws when applying them and that significant judgements can set precedents that bind future courts.
width.typical: Explain the roles of statutory interpretation and precedent in the development of law; describe how a significant judgement (e.g. the Mabo Case 1992) overturned an established legal concept and created new law; discuss how this illustrates the law-making function of courts alongside parliament.
wider: Trace the legal legacy of the Mabo Case through subsequent native title legislation and cases, assessing how one precedent reshaped an entire area of law
Investigate a more recent High Court decision (e.g. LGBTIQ+ rights, immigration, corporate liability) and explain how it changed or clarified the law
Compare the doctrine of precedent in Australia's common law system with the approach in a civil law country and evaluate the advantages of each

modes.reason: Precedent is conceptually demanding — students need to understand that a judgement in one case constrains decisions in future unrelated cases. Unpacking the logic of why judges follow precedent (legal certainty, equality) is worth explicit investment before students engage with specific cases.

descriptors.title: Trials, roles and rights
descriptors.description: the role of courts, judges, lawyers and juries in trials, and the rights of the accused and the rights of victims
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the structure of the court hierarchy and the difference between civil and criminal law from AC9HC9K03. They have a surface-level understanding of courts as places where law is applied but have not yet examined who does what inside a trial or what rights attach to participants.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles of courts, judges, lawyers and juries in criminal and civil trials, compare the rights of the accused with the rights of victims, and evaluate whether the legal system delivers equal access to justice.

nodes.label: Roles within trials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the roles of judges, lawyers, court officials and juries in criminal and civil trials.
criteria: Describes the role of the judge in a trial
Describes the role of the jury or lawyer and explains how it differs from the judge's role

width.minimum: Describe the role of the judge and at least one other participant (lawyer or jury) in a criminal trial.
width.typical: Investigate the roles of judges, lawyers (prosecution/plaintiff, defence), court officials, and juries in both criminal and civil trials; explain how each contributes to the trial process and to the delivery of justice.
wider: Compare the role of the jury in a criminal trial with the role of the judge alone in a civil matter, and evaluate when each approach is more appropriate
Investigate the history of jury trials and examine arguments for and against the jury system in contemporary Australia
Examine how magistrates courts operate without juries and assess the implications for defendants

modes.reason: Students benefit from building a clear repertoire of participant roles before comparing rights across those roles. Confusion between the judge's role and the jury's role is a common error that undermines the rights analysis in Node 2.

nodes.label: Rights of the accused and victims
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the rights of the accused with the rights of victims in criminal trials, and identify the rights of parties in civil cases.
criteria: Names at least two rights of the accused in a criminal trial and explains their purpose
Identifies at least one right or protection available to victims and compares it with a corresponding right of the accused
nodes.hinge_reason: The tension between rights of the accused and rights of victims is the conceptual core of this standard, and thin understanding here means students cannot engage with the access-to-justice analysis in Node 3. Students who reduce rights to 'accused has all the rights' or 'victims are left out' cannot evaluate the system's fairness.

width.minimum: Identify at least two rights of the accused in a criminal trial (e.g. right to silence, presumption of innocence) and state one right afforded to victims.
width.typical: Compare the rights of the accused with the rights of victims in criminal trials, including presumption of innocence, right to silence, right to legal representation, and the role of victim impact statements; compare the rights of plaintiff and defendant in a civil case; explain the role of the police in enabling equal treatment under the law.
wider: Examine cases where the rights of victims and rights of the accused have been argued to conflict, and evaluate how the legal system attempts to balance them
Investigate how victim support services and restorative justice approaches seek to address limitations in formal victim rights
Compare rights of the accused in Australia with those in another jurisdiction (e.g. the USA) and evaluate differences

modes.reason: Students often assume the presumption of innocence privileges the accused at the expense of victims. Unpacking why these procedural protections exist (preventing wrongful conviction) before comparing them with victim entitlements produces more nuanced analysis.
Working through specific case types — a domestic violence case, a property crime case — that make rights concrete helps students move past the abstract definitions and into evaluation.

nodes.label: Access to justice and equality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate barriers to equal access to justice and evaluate whether civil remedies and appeals deliver just outcomes.
criteria: Identifies at least two barriers to equal access to justice and explains how each limits participation in the legal system
Explains how legal aid or civil appeals contribute to (or fall short of) equalising access to justice

width.minimum: Identify at least two barriers to equal access to justice (e.g. cost, geographic isolation, literacy, race or ethnicity) and explain how they affect access.
width.typical: Investigate potential barriers to equality of access to justice including financial constraints, education and literacy, geographic location, and racial or ethnic background (especially for First Nations Australians); explain the purpose of civil remedies and rights of appeal; evaluate whether legal aid contributes meaningfully to addressing inequality of access.
wider: Investigate the specific barriers facing First Nations Australians in accessing the legal system and assess what systemic changes have been made or proposed
Compare legal aid funding and scope in Australia with another country and evaluate the implications for access to justice
Examine a case where a wrongful conviction resulted from inadequate legal representation and assess what systemic failures it revealed

modes.reason: Access to justice barriers are most visible through specific population groups and geographic contexts. Examining barriers for rural communities alongside barriers for First Nations Australians demonstrates that access inequality has multiple intersecting causes.

descriptors.title: Civic and global participation
descriptors.description: how and why individuals and groups, including community, religious and cultural groups, participate in and contribute to civic life in Australia and to global citizenship
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how culture and religion influence individuals' and groups' perceptions and expressions of citizenship (AC9HC8K05), and have examined debates about national identity and citizenship (AC9HC8K06). They understand that citizenship is expressed through identity and culture but have not yet examined formal and informal mechanisms of civic participation at community, national and global levels.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how and why individuals and groups participate in civic life in Australia and as global citizens, including the contribution of community, religious and cultural organisations.

nodes.label: Forms and motivations of civic participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different forms of civic participation and explain the motivations that lead individuals and groups to participate.
criteria: Names at least two different forms of civic participation at different levels (local, national, or global)
Explains at least one motivation that leads an individual or group to participate civically

width.minimum: Identify at least two different forms of civic participation (e.g. voting, volunteering, activism, charitable work) and explain why individuals or groups participate.
width.typical: Describe formal and informal forms of civic participation; explain motivations for participation including community responsibility, religious obligation, cultural identity, and personal commitment; distinguish between local, national and global levels of civic engagement.
wider: Investigate historical examples of civic movements in Australia (e.g. the 1967 referendum campaign, women's suffrage) and compare their methods and motivations with contemporary civic participation
Compare the civic participation frameworks in Australia with another democracy and assess how institutional structures shape participation
Examine barriers to civic participation for marginalised groups and evaluate strategies that have increased inclusion

modes.reason: Students tend to think of civic participation as voting or protesting. Building a broader repertoire of participation forms — including volunteering, faith-based service, online advocacy, community organising — provides the range needed for Node 2's case analysis.

nodes.label: Community, religious and cultural groups in civic life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can research and explain the contribution of specific non-government organisations, community or religious groups to Australian civic life.
criteria: Describes the work of at least one specific Australian NGO, community or religious group
Explains the extent of its contribution to civic life with reference to a specific activity or outcome

width.minimum: Research one specific Australian NGO, community group or religious organisation and explain its contribution to civic life.
width.typical: Research the work of Australian NGOs, philanthropists, community groups and religious groups; explain the extent to which they contribute to the Australian community; include examples from different types of organisations (faith-based, secular, community-led); consider how different groups respond to different community needs.
wider: Compare the civic contributions of a faith-based organisation (e.g. Salvation Army, Sikh Volunteers Australia) with a secular NGO (e.g. Red Cross, Oxfam) and evaluate how their motivations and methods differ
Investigate an organisation that specifically supports First Nations Australian communities and assess how it complements or fills gaps in government services
Examine how the SES or another emergency volunteer organisation contributes to civic resilience and evaluate what makes its model effective

modes.reason: Students who research only one type of organisation tend to generalise its model to all civic participation. Examining two or three contrasting organisations (e.g. one faith-based, one secular, one focused on First Nations communities) develops more nuanced understanding of the diversity of civic contribution.

nodes.label: Global citizenship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what global citizenship means and provide examples of individuals or groups acting as global citizens.
criteria: Explains what global citizenship means in their own words
Identifies at least one example of an individual or group acting as a global citizen and explains what makes their actions an expression of global citizenship

width.minimum: Explain what it means to be a global citizen and identify one example of a person or group acting as a global citizen.
width.typical: Research examples of young people acting as global citizens (e.g. Malala Yousafzai, Greta Thunberg, Amelia Telford, Bassam Maaliki); explain what distinguishes global citizenship from national civic participation; discuss how global citizenship connects to issues such as sustainability, climate change, and human rights.
wider: Investigate the work of UNICEF Youth Ambassadors or equivalent programs and evaluate how they build global citizenship capacity in young people
Examine a global citizenship campaign on a sustainability or climate issue and assess what made it effective or ineffective at driving change
Compare the concept of global citizenship across different cultural frameworks and evaluate whether it is a universal or Western-centric concept

modes.reason: Global citizenship risks being abstract without concrete examples. Using examples of young Australians alongside international figures makes the concept accessible and avoids the misconception that global citizenship requires celebrity status.

descriptors.title: Media influence on identity and diversity
descriptors.description: the influence of a range of media, including social media, in shaping identity and attitudes to diversity
descriptors.knowledge: Students have examined different experiences of and debates about Australia's national identity and citizenship including perspectives of First Nations Australians and migrant groups (AC9HC8K06). They understand identity as shaped by culture and community but have not yet examined how media actively constructs and circulates representations that shape identity and attitudes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how media, including social media, influences the shaping of identity and attitudes to diversity, and analyse media representations of different groups in Australian society.

nodes.label: How media constructs representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how media construct representations of groups and why these representations matter for community attitudes.
criteria: Explains that media representations involve active choices about framing and selection
Identifies a specific example of media representation of a group and explains how it shapes community attitudes
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat media representations as neutral descriptions rather than constructed artefacts, they cannot undertake the social media analysis in Node 2, which depends on understanding media choices as active shaping forces rather than mirrors of community attitudes.

width.minimum: Explain that media do not simply report reality but make choices about how to represent groups, and identify at least one example of a media representation of a specific group.
width.typical: Analyse how media represent different groups in Australian society — including First Nations Australians, immigrant groups, male and female sporting figures, and people with disability; explain how these representations are constructed through selection, framing and emphasis; identify the impact those representations can have on community attitudes.
wider: Compare how the same group (e.g. a refugee community, First Nations Australians) is represented across different media outlets and evaluate what drives the differences
Trace how representations of a specific group have changed over time and assess what has driven that change
Examine representations in advertising or entertainment media and assess how they shape or challenge stereotypes about gender, ethnicity or disability

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding on the distinction between representation and reality — that the same event or community can be represented in multiple ways, and that choices about framing carry consequences. A comparative analysis exercise (same event, two different outlets) makes this concrete.

nodes.label: Social media, identity and human rights campaigns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how social media influences identity formation and explain how human rights campaigns use social media to engage the public.
criteria: Identifies at least one way social media influences identity or attitudes to diversity
Describes a human rights campaign that used social media and explains how it sought to engage public participation

width.minimum: Identify at least one way social media influences identity and one way it has been used in a human rights campaign.
width.typical: Investigate how social media shapes identity (including the construction of personal and group identity online) and attitudes to diversity; investigate a human rights campaign that uses social media and how members of the public have engaged with the issue; assess both the reach and the limitations of social media as a tool for civic engagement.
wider: Analyse a specific social media campaign on a human rights or diversity issue (e.g. #BlackLivesMatter, #MeToo, LGBTIQ+ campaigns) and evaluate its impact on public attitudes and policy
Investigate how algorithms shape what content people see and how this can create filter bubbles that reinforce existing identity and attitudes
Examine how social media platforms are used by both those advocating for diversity and those spreading divisive or hateful content, and evaluate what responsibilities platforms have

modes.reason: Social media's role in identity is experienced differently by students in different communities. Using both a national-scale campaign and a local or youth-focused example makes the analysis personally anchored and more critical.

descriptors.title: Develop and modify civic inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop and modify questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues (AC9HC8S01). At Year 9 the expectation adds modification — students are expected to revisit and refine questions as their investigation develops, not just formulate them at the outset.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop initial inquiry questions about Australia's political and legal systems or civic issues, and modify those questions as their investigation develops in response to new information.

nodes.label: Developing focused civic inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop focused, investigable questions about Australia's political and legal systems or a contemporary civic issue.
criteria: Develops at least one inquiry question that is focused on a political, legal or civic issue and requires analysis rather than a simple factual answer
Explains why the question is worth investigating
nodes.hinge_reason: A poorly scoped initial question prevents meaningful modification — students cannot improve a question that was never adequately formulated. If the initial question is too vague or simply factual, the modification work in Node 2 has nothing to build on and the investigation cannot proceed purposefully.

width.minimum: Develop at least one question that is focused enough to investigate (not too broad, not a yes/no question) about a political, legal or civic topic.
width.typical: Develop focused inquiry questions about Australia's political and legal systems or civic issues; distinguish between questions that can be answered with facts and questions that require analysis and evaluation; practise constructing questions using the elaboration examples (e.g. 'How democratic is Australia's system of government?' or 'Does Australia's legal system deliver justice?').
wider: Develop question sets at different levels of abstraction (factual, analytical, evaluative) for the same civic topic and assess how each type drives different kinds of investigation
Practise developing inquiry questions from news events or policy changes, evaluating what makes a civic question worth investigating
Compare student-generated questions with those from published civic education inquiries and evaluate the differences in focus and scope

modes.reason: Students need explicit practice distinguishing researchable analytical questions from vague or simply factual ones. Working through several examples — identifying what makes each stronger or weaker — builds the judgment needed before they formulate their own inquiry questions.

nodes.label: Modifying questions as investigation develops
nodes.checkpoint: Students can revisit and modify their inquiry questions in response to new information gathered during investigation.
criteria: Modifies at least one inquiry question during an investigation
Explains what new information or understanding prompted the modification and how the revised question better serves the investigation

width.minimum: Modify at least one inquiry question based on information gathered during investigation, and explain what prompted the change.
width.typical: Revisit initial inquiry questions as investigation develops; modify questions to be more specific, more accurate, or more relevant based on what has been found; explain the reasoning for modifications (e.g. moving from 'How democratic is Australia's system of government?' to 'How representative is Australia's system of government?' as evidence about voting systems is encountered).
wider: Document a full inquiry question development trail — initial question, modification trigger, revised question, and effect on investigation — and evaluate how modification improved the inquiry
Practise modifying questions across two or three different civic topics to build flexibility and transfer
Evaluate the inquiry questions used in a published report or civic inquiry and propose how they could have been better framed

modes.reason: Modifying questions requires students to hold their original question in mind, identify the specific gap or imprecision the new information revealed, and articulate the revision clearly. Regular low-stakes practice — e.g. modifying questions at the end of each research session — builds this reflective habit.

descriptors.title: Locate, select and compare information
descriptors.description: locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources (AC9HC8S02). At Year 9 the expectation advances from organising to comparing — students are expected to evaluate relative accuracy and reliability across sources, not just find and sort relevant information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources, evaluating the accuracy and reliability of different sources.

nodes.label: Locating and selecting relevant information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate information from a range of source types and select what is relevant to their inquiry.
criteria: Locates information on a civic issue from at least two different source types
Identifies which information is most relevant to the inquiry question and explains the selection

width.minimum: Locate information on a civic, political or legal issue from at least two different source types (e.g. a government website and a news article) and select information relevant to the inquiry question.
width.typical: Locate information from a range of print and online source types — including statistics, graphs, tables, maps, articles, blogs and advertisements — and select relevant information or data about a civic issue; explain why some sources are more relevant than others for a specific inquiry question.
wider: Locate information from primary sources (e.g. parliamentary Hansard, legislation, court judgements) alongside secondary sources and compare what each type offers for civic inquiry
Investigate how to access government data sets or ABS statistics and use them to support analysis of a civic issue
Practise locating information on a contentious civic issue (e.g. water policy, COVID policy) across multiple source types and assess which source types are most informative

modes.reason: Students default to search engines and Wikipedia. Building familiarity with a wider repertoire of source types — government databases, Hansard, NGO reports, statistical data sets — is prerequisite to the comparative analysis in Node 2.

nodes.label: Comparing accuracy and reliability across sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare sources and explain why some have greater accuracy and reliability than others for a given civic inquiry.
criteria: Compares at least two sources on a civic issue and explains which is more reliable and why
Applies at least two evaluative criteria (e.g. authority, currency, bias, purpose) when comparing sources

width.minimum: Compare two sources on the same civic issue and explain why one has greater accuracy or reliability than the other.
width.typical: Identify why some sources and information have greater accuracy and reliability than others; apply criteria such as authority, currency, bias, purpose, and evidence base to evaluate sources; compare across source types (e.g. government reports vs opinion pieces vs social media posts); explain how source reliability varies by inquiry question.
wider: Evaluate sources on a specific contested civic issue (e.g. Indigenous rights, refugee policy, climate legislation) where sources reflect strongly opposed perspectives, and assess how to use each appropriately
Investigate how misinformation circulates on civic topics and develop criteria for identifying unreliable sources in a social media context
Compare Australian and international sources on the same civic issue and evaluate how national context affects source perspective and reliability

modes.reason: Comparing source reliability is a reasoning task, not a checklist exercise. Students need explicit practice applying evaluative criteria to real source comparisons — particularly for sources where bias is subtle or where authority and motivation conflict.

descriptors.title: Evaluate civic perspectives and interpretations
descriptors.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse information about civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges (AC9HC8S03). At Year 9 the expectation advances from explaining differences to evaluating them — students must assess the values, motivations and contexts that underpin perspectives, not just identify that perspectives differ.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse information about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, including examining the values and motivations underlying those perspectives.

nodes.label: Identifying values and motivations underlying perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the values, motivations and contexts that underpin different perspectives on a civic or political issue.
criteria: Identifies at least two perspectives on a civic issue
Explains the value or motivation underlying each perspective, not just the position held
nodes.hinge_reason: If students can only identify that perspectives differ without understanding why, the evaluation in Node 2 is superficial — they end up comparing conclusions rather than reasoning. Evaluation requires understanding that perspectives are grounded in values and contexts, not just positions.

width.minimum: Identify the values or motivations underlying at least two different perspectives on a civic or political issue.
width.typical: Identify the values, motivations and contexts that underpin different perspectives about political and legal systems and processes; explain why the same information can be interpreted differently depending on perspective; apply this to at least one substantive civic issue (e.g. constitutional recognition for First Nations Australians, impacts of mining activity on communities).
wider: Investigate a civic issue where perspectives divide along lines of lived experience (e.g. First Nations Australians' perspectives on constitutional recognition versus non-Indigenous perspectives) and analyse how context shapes interpretation
Examine a historical civic issue and a contemporary one to compare whether the values underpinning key perspectives have changed over time
Map perspectives on a policy debate using a values framework (e.g. liberty, equality, community, authority) to evaluate what is really at stake in the disagreement

modes.reason: The move from 'these perspectives differ' to 'these perspectives differ because they prioritise different values' is the key analytical step. Students benefit from an explicit scaffold that asks: what does this perspective assume? What does it prioritise? What would challenge it?

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness and policy responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a political or legal institution and examine how government responds to civic issues.
criteria: Evaluates at least one perspective on the effectiveness of a political or legal institution using evidence
Examines a government response to a civic issue and identifies at least two different perspectives on its effectiveness

width.minimum: Examine at least one perspective on the effectiveness of a political or legal institution and explain the basis for that assessment.
width.typical: Examine information including diverse perspectives about the effectiveness of a political or legal institution (e.g. 'Is Australia's parliament representative of the Australian community?' or 'Does the court system deliver justice for victims of crime?'); investigate how the Australian Government responds to a civic issue and examine the policy development and implementation process; evaluate the quality of different perspectives using evidence.
wider: Investigate a government policy response to a major civic issue (e.g. welfare reform in response to economic crisis, health policy during COVID) and evaluate its effectiveness from multiple stakeholder perspectives
Examine a case where natural disaster or emergency response policy was evaluated differently by different communities (e.g. rural vs urban, First Nations vs non-Indigenous) and analyse why
Assess the effectiveness of a political institution (e.g. the Senate, an ombudsman office) using criteria drawn from multiple civic perspectives including those of underrepresented groups

modes.reason: Evaluation is stronger when students have multiple policy contexts to draw on. Using two contrasting cases — one where government response was broadly effective, one where it was contested or inadequate — develops evaluative flexibility.

descriptors.title: Evaluate civic participation methods
descriptors.description: evaluate the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation (AC9HC8S04). At Year 9 the expectation advances from explaining to evaluating — students must assess whether methods are effective and what their intended and unintended effects are.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate the methods or strategies used in civic participation decisions, assess intended and unintended effects of action plans, and develop evaluated plans for addressing a contemporary civic issue.

nodes.label: Examining civic action plans
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a government or community action plan, identifying its actions, measures, and intended and unintended effects.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific actions in a civic action plan
Identifies at least one intended effect and one measure used to track it
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to identify actions, measures, and effects is prerequisite to developing an evaluated plan in Node 2. Students who cannot distinguish a measure (how progress is tracked) from an action (what is done) cannot build evaluation criteria into their own planning.

width.minimum: Examine one government or community action plan and identify its intended goals and at least one measure used to achieve them.
width.typical: Examine a government action plan and identify the actions, the measures, and the intended and unintended effects of the plan; use examples such as a local recycling program, a national literacy campaign, or a waste reduction strategy; explain how intended and unintended effects are discovered and how they should inform future planning.
wider: Compare two civic action plans on the same issue (e.g. two different government approaches to reducing plastic waste) and evaluate which methods were more effective and why
Investigate how a government action plan has been evaluated over time and assess whether evaluation data led to changes in method
Examine an action plan that produced significant unintended negative effects and analyse what evaluation processes could have identified the risk earlier

modes.reason: Students frequently conflate 'what we will do' with 'how we will know it worked'. An explicit scaffold that separates action → measure → intended effect → evaluation builds the analytical vocabulary needed for Node 2's planning work.

nodes.label: Developing and evaluating a civic participation plan
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a plan to address a contemporary civic issue that incorporates a consultation process and evaluation criteria.
criteria: Develops a plan that includes at least one action, one consultation mechanism, and one evaluation criterion
Explains how the consultation process ensures a range of views will be represented

width.minimum: Develop a basic plan to address a civic issue that includes at least one action, one measure of success, and one way to consult stakeholders.
width.typical: Develop a plan of action to address a contemporary civic issue that incorporates a consultation process to ensure a range of views are heard, and participants are provided with opportunities to contribute; include evaluation criteria for assessing effectiveness; consider examples such as a local safety campaign, a community sustainability initiative, or an educational resources strategy.
wider: Develop and peer-review plans for addressing the same civic issue using different methods (e.g. media campaign vs community consultation vs policy advocacy) and evaluate which approach best fits the context
Evaluate government media campaigns and community activities used over time to address a recurring civic issue (e.g. littering, road safety) and determine which have been most effective and why
Incorporate feedback loops into a civic plan — specifying how the plan would be revised if early evaluation data indicated it was not working

modes.reason: Developing a plan integrates the analytical skills from Node 1 (examining existing plans) with the capability skills of civic planning. Students are executing a genuine mode B task — the thinking is only legible through the plan they produce.

Plans developed for contrasting civic contexts (a local personal safety issue, an international development or aid context) build transferability — students learn that civic planning methods must be adapted to context, not just applied formulaically.

descriptors.title: Create evidence-based civic arguments
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate evidence
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence (AC9HC8S05). At Year 9 the expectation advances from referencing to incorporating evidence — evidence should be integrated into the argument structure rather than added as a gesture.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms, with evidence incorporated into the argument structure.

nodes.label: Using civic concepts and terms accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can accurately apply civics and citizenship concepts and terms in their written or oral responses.
criteria: Uses at least three civics and citizenship terms accurately in context
The terms are applied to demonstrate understanding, not simply defined

width.minimum: Use at least three civics and citizenship terms accurately in a written or oral response on a civic topic.
width.typical: Use civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in descriptions, explanations and arguments, including terms such as 'representative', 'jurisdictions', 'parliamentary majority', 'mandate', 'precedent', 'presumption of innocence'; demonstrate understanding of the term through accurate application rather than definition alone.
wider: Practise using civic concepts and terms in varied contexts — applying the same term in different argument types (description, explanation, evaluation) to build flexible understanding
Examine how civic concepts are used (and sometimes misused) in media and political discourse, and evaluate the implications for public understanding
Build a personal civics glossary with examples of correct use drawn from real civic sources such as court judgements, parliamentary debate or policy documents

modes.reason: Accurate use of civic terminology requires regular, low-stakes application across multiple contexts. Students who are only exposed to terms in definition exercises often misapply them in extended writing — deliberate practice in varied written tasks builds accuracy.

nodes.label: Incorporating evidence into civic arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a civic argument in which evidence is incorporated into the argument structure, not merely appended.
criteria: Constructs an argument on a civic issue that includes at least one claim and one piece of supporting evidence
Evidence is integrated into the argument (supports a claim) rather than simply listed or appended
Uses at least two civics and citizenship terms accurately within the argument

width.minimum: Construct an argument on a civic issue that includes at least one piece of evidence integrated into the body of the argument (not just listed at the end).
width.typical: Develop an evidence-based argument about a civics and citizenship issue — such as a need to reform youth justice arrangements in a particular jurisdiction; incorporate evidence into the argument structure by using it to support claims, acknowledge counter-arguments, and draw conclusions; use civic concepts and terms throughout.
wider: Develop arguments on the same civic issue from opposing perspectives, and evaluate which argument makes more effective use of evidence
Construct an argument that responds to a counter-argument — specifically addressing contrary evidence rather than ignoring it

Develop a multimodal civic argument (written, visual, or oral) for a specific audience (e.g. a parliamentary submission, a community presentation, a letter to a local councillor) and evaluate how audience shapes argument construction

modes.reason: Evidence incorporation is an integration task — students must combine their civic content knowledge, their source evaluation skills (AC9HC9S02), and their perspective analysis skills (AC9HC9S03) in the production of a single argument. Feedback on drafts that distinguishes evidence integration from evidence reference is the key teaching move.

descriptors.title: Comparing systems of government
descriptors.description: the key features and values of Australia's system of government compared with at least one other democratic or non-democratic system of government in the Asia-Pacific region
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the role of the Australian Constitution in providing the basis for Australia's federal system and democratic processes, including institutions and the referendum process (AC9HC9K01). They understand the legislative processes through which federal government policy is shaped and implemented (AC9HC9K02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare the key features and values of Australia's system of government with at least one other system of government in the Asia-Pacific region, explaining similarities, differences and cultural influences.

nodes.label: Key features of Australia's system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the key institutional features and values of Australia's system of government, including free and fair elections, the party system, separation of powers, the rule of law, and protection of human rights.
criteria: Identifies and accurately describes at least three key features of Australia's system of government
Explains a democratic value that underpins at least one of those features
Uses appropriate civics terminology (e.g. separation of powers, rule of law)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot accurately characterise Australia's own system will make false comparisons in subsequent nodes — misidentifying similarities and differences based on misconceptions about the Australian baseline.

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least three key institutional features of Australia's system of government using accurate civics terminology.
width.typical: Explain the full set of key features — elections, party system, partial separation of powers, rule of law, and human rights protections — and the democratic values underpinning them.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians have historically engaged with and been affected by Australia's political institutions, and compare with Indigenous peoples' political participation in another nation
Investigate how Australia's federal structure distributes power between Commonwealth and states, and trace how this emerged from colonial history
Explore the role of the Westminster tradition in shaping Australian democratic norms and compare with a presidential system

modes.reason: Students often conflate features (e.g. treating separation of powers as complete rather than partial) or conflate values with structures. Invest time unpacking the distinction between institutional mechanisms and underlying democratic values before comparison begins.
Width across multiple features (elections, law, rights protections) ensures students have a usable comparative framework rather than a single point of comparison.

nodes.label: Features of a comparison system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the key features of at least one other system of government in the Asia-Pacific region, identifying whether it is democratic or non-democratic.
criteria: Describes at least three key institutional features of the selected comparison system
Classifies the system as democratic or non-democratic and provides at least one reason
Uses appropriate civics terminology to describe the comparison system

width.minimum: Describe at least three key institutional features of one selected comparison system, identifying whether it is democratic or non-democratic.
width.typical: Describe the key features of a selected Asia-Pacific system of government — including electoral processes (or lack thereof), structure of power, rule of law, and rights protections — and classify it as democratic or non-democratic with reasons.
wider: Investigate the political system of an additional Asia-Pacific nation to enable a three-way comparison
Examine how cultural, historical or colonial factors shaped the comparison system's current political structures
Research the experiences of Indigenous peoples in the comparison nation's political system and evaluate the degree of their inclusion

modes.reason: Students benefit from building a repertoire of examples from the Asia-Pacific region — even minimal exposure to two or three systems before selecting one for deep comparison gives them more informed selection criteria.

nodes.label: Structured comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the key features and values of Australia's system with the selected comparison system, identifying specific similarities and differences across multiple dimensions.
criteria: Identifies at least two structural similarities and two structural differences between the two systems
Connects at least one difference to an underlying democratic or non-democratic value
Uses specific evidence or examples from both systems to support the comparison
nodes.hinge_reason: The comparison move is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who produce surface-level comparison (listing features without connecting them to underlying values) will not satisfy the descriptor's 'key features and values' framing — the integration node cannot recover this gap.

width.minimum: Identify at least two similarities and two differences between Australia's system and the comparison system, using a structured framework (e.g. table, structured paragraph).
width.typical: Compare Australia's system with the selected system across multiple dimensions — electoral processes, structure of power, rule of law, and rights protections — explaining both structural differences and the values that underpin them.
wider: Compare the experiences of First Nations Australians in engaging with the Australian political system with those of Indigenous peoples in the comparison nation
Evaluate which system better protects human rights for minority groups, drawing on specific evidence
Investigate how global interconnectedness (international agreements, trade, migration) has influenced political similarities between the two systems

modes.reason: Students often list differences without explaining the values or institutional logic behind them. Use structured scaffolds (e.g. comparative frameworks) to push students from feature-matching to values-based analysis.
Widening to include First Nations political participation or rights-minority analysis gives students comparison across multiple values dimensions, not just structural features.

nodes.label: Cultural influences on political systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural influences have shaped Australia's political system and that of the comparison country, reflecting on what this reveals about the relationship between culture and governance.
criteria: Identifies a specific cultural or historical influence on each system's political design
Explains how that influence connects to a visible feature or value of the system
Reflects on what the comparison reveals about the relationship between culture and governance

width.minimum: Identify at least one cultural or historical influence that has shaped Australia's political system and one that has shaped the comparison system.
width.typical: Explore and reflect on the cultural, historical and social influences shaping both political systems, explaining how these influences account for key differences in values and institutional design.
wider: Investigate how colonialism has shaped political institutions in both countries and the ongoing implications for First Nations or Indigenous peoples
Compare how religious, philosophical or ethnic diversity is managed differently in each system and what this reveals about democratic values
Examine how recent political change (e.g. constitutional reform, protest movements) reflects cultural values in one of the two nations

modes.reason: This node integrates feature knowledge, comparative skills, and cultural reasoning into a reflective account. Students are synthesising earlier nodes rather than adding new factual content — the teaching investment is in supporting that synthesis.

descriptors.title: Regional and global government roles
descriptors.description: the Australian Government's role and responsibilities at a regional and global level
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in civic life in Australia and contribute to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand legislative processes shaping government policy (AC9HC9K02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the Australian Government's role and responsibilities at a regional and global level, analysing and evaluating its participation in relation to a global issue.

nodes.label: Forms of regional and global participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the main ways Australia contributes to and participates in the Asia-Pacific region and globally, including membership of international organisations and agreements.
criteria: Names at least three distinct forms of Australia's regional or global participation
Provides a specific example for at least two of those forms
Distinguishes between regional (Asia-Pacific) and global participation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have only vague knowledge of participation forms cannot complete the evaluative analysis in subsequent nodes — they lack the factual base to assess effectiveness or compare responses.

width.minimum: Identify at least three specific forms of Australia's regional or global participation (e.g. peacekeeping, development aid, UN involvement) with brief descriptions of each.
width.typical: Explain the full range of ways Australia participates in the Asia-Pacific region and globally — exchange programs, peacekeeping, election monitoring, development aid, health programs, disaster management, and international treaty participation including the UN Security Council — using accurate examples.
wider: Investigate Australia's participation in a specific multilateral body (e.g. UN Security Council, G20) and evaluate what membership requires and delivers
Research how Australia's engagement with the Asia-Pacific has changed over time and what this reveals about shifting foreign policy priorities
Examine how Australia's international development commitments compare with those of comparable nations (e.g. aid spending as percentage of GNI)

modes.reason: Build a concrete repertoire of participation types and examples before moving to evaluation. Students should be able to name specific programs or agreements, not just categories.

nodes.label: International treaty obligations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain Australia's responsibilities and commitments under key international treaties and conventions, using specific examples.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific treaty or convention and explains what it requires of Australia
Explains how the treaty has shaped at least one aspect of Australian law or government policy
Distinguishes between Australia's commitments and its actions in at least one case
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding treaty obligations is prerequisite to evaluating Australia's participation — students cannot assess effectiveness without knowing what commitments Australia has made. This directly feeds AC9HC10K04 as well.

width.minimum: Explain Australia's responsibilities under at least one international treaty or convention, identifying what the commitment requires of the Australian Government.
width.typical: Investigate Australia's responsibilities under two or more international treaties or conventions (e.g. UN Sustainable Development Agenda, UNFCCC, Refugee Convention, UNDRIP) and explain how each shapes Australian law or government policy.
wider: Examine how the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples has shaped (or not shaped) Australian policy toward First Nations Australians
Compare the binding vs advisory nature of different international instruments and what this means for Australia's obligations
Investigate a case where Australia has been criticised for failing to meet its international obligations and analyse the government's response

modes.reason: Students often conflate signing, ratifying and implementing treaties, or assume all international agreements are equally binding. Invest in clarifying the legal status and practical requirements of different instruments.
The UNDRIP direction is particularly rich — it connects treaty obligations to First Nations Australians' lived experience and to the descriptor's explicit inclusion of First Nations contexts.

nodes.label: Analysing and evaluating global participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse and evaluate the reasons for and effectiveness of Australia's participation in the region and globally with regard to a specific global issue.
criteria: Analyses at least two reasons for Australia's participation in relation to a named global issue
Provides a supported evaluative judgement about the effectiveness of that participation
Acknowledges at least one limitation or competing perspective in the evaluation

width.minimum: Analyse Australia's participation in relation to one global issue, identifying reasons for involvement and offering a supported judgement about its effectiveness.
width.typical: Analyse and evaluate the reasons for and effectiveness of Australia's participation in the region or globally with regard to a significant global issue (e.g. human rights, climate, conflict, democratic challenges), including consideration of competing perspectives and evidence.
wider: Compare the responses of different governments and organisations to the same global issue and evaluate why responses differ
Investigate how global interconnectedness both creates and helps solve the issue being studied
Evaluate the impact of the issue on First Nations Australians' reconciliation, truth-telling and sovereignty alongside its broader impact on Australian identity

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to weigh evidence and acknowledge competing views. Support students in distinguishing description of actions from evaluation of effectiveness — these are different claims requiring different evidence.
Widening the issue context (e.g. examining climate plus human rights rather than one alone) gives students comparative material for more nuanced evaluation.

nodes.label: Global interconnectedness and Australia's choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how global interconnectedness affects Australia's capacity to address global issues, and evaluate how this shapes Australian identity and policy choices.
criteria: Explains at least one way global interconnectedness enables and one way it constrains Australia's response to a global issue
Connects Australia's global participation to its national identity or values
Evaluates the implications for citizens acting in the global interest

width.minimum: Explain how global interconnectedness has either helped or hindered Australia's ability to respond to a global issue.
width.typical: Identify and explain how the forces of global interconnectedness both exacerbate and enhance Australia's ability to address a key global issue, and evaluate impacts on Australia's identity and citizens' choices to act in the global interest.
wider: Investigate a specific case where Australia's international trade relationships have created tensions with its stated commitment to human rights
Examine how diaspora communities in Australia influence Australian foreign policy choices in relation to their countries of origin
Evaluate how the concept of global citizenship has evolved and what it demands of Australian citizens specifically

modes.reason: This node brings together participation knowledge, treaty obligations, and evaluative reasoning into a reflective account of Australia's global position and identity. Teaching investment is in supporting synthesis rather than adding factual content.

descriptors.title: Parliament, High Court and rights
descriptors.description: the role of the parliament and the High Court of Australia in protecting rights under the Constitution, common law, and through federal and state statute law
descriptors.knowledge: Students know the key features and jurisdictions of Australia's court system and the operations of courts and tribunals (AC9HC9K03). They understand the role of courts, judges, lawyers and juries in trials, and the rights of the accused and victims (AC9HC9K04).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles of both parliament and the High Court in protecting rights through the Constitution, common law, and statute law, comparing different mechanisms and their effectiveness.

nodes.label: Sources of rights protection in Australia
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the three main sources of rights protection in Australia — the Constitution, common law, and statute law — and explain how each operates.
criteria: Correctly identifies all three sources of rights protection in Australia
Explains how at least two of the three sources operate to protect rights
Distinguishes between constitutional rights and legislated rights
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate the three sources — or who don't understand the distinction between constitutional, common law and statutory rights — will misattribute the role of parliament vs High Court in subsequent nodes, undermining the whole comparison.

width.minimum: Identify the three sources of rights protection (Constitution, common law, statute law) and explain in basic terms how each provides protection.
width.typical: Explain how the Constitution, common law, and federal and state statute law each protect rights, including the nature of express versus implied constitutional rights, judge-made common law rights, and legislated rights.
wider: Compare Australia's approach to rights protection (without a bill of rights) with a constitutional bill of rights (e.g. USA) and a statutory bill of rights (e.g. New Zealand), evaluating the strengths and limitations of each
Investigate what 'express rights' and 'implied rights' mean in the Australian constitutional context using specific historical examples
Explore why Australia does not have a national bill of rights and analyse the arguments for and against introducing one

modes.reason: The three-source framework requires clear categorical distinctions. Students commonly conflate common law and statute law, or assume the Constitution is the only source. Scaffolded comparison of all three before examining specific cases reduces confusion.
Comparing with the US and NZ models gives students a clear external reference point that makes Australia's unusual rights framework more legible.

nodes.label: Role of the High Court in interpreting and applying law
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role of the High Court in interpreting and applying the law, and identify examples of High Court decisions that have shaped rights protection.
criteria: Explains the High Court's role in interpreting and applying the law
Identifies at least one case in which the High Court's interpretation shaped rights protection
Explains what the court decided and the significance of that decision for rights
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand the High Court's interpretive role — that it applies existing law rather than making policy, but its interpretations can effectively create new rights — will not be able to accurately compare the parliament's and court's roles in the final node.

width.minimum: Explain the High Court's role in interpreting the Constitution and applying the law, using at least one contemporary or significant case as an example.
width.typical: Explain the role of the High Court in interpreting and applying the law, including exploration of express and implied constitutional rights through significant cases (e.g. Kruger v the Commonwealth, Roach v Electoral Commissioner, Mabo).
wider: Investigate how the Native Title Act 1993 emerged from High Court interpretation of common law in Mabo, and how it then became enshrined in statutory law — tracing the pathway from case to legislation
Research how the Stolen Generations Case (Kruger v the Commonwealth) and the Vicki Lee Roach Case shaped understanding of implied rights in Australia
Examine a recent High Court decision and analyse how it changed or clarified existing rights protections

modes.reason: Students commonly misunderstand the distinction between judicial interpretation and legislative change. Invest in the 'how courts create law through interpretation' concept before examining specific cases.
The Mabo to Native Title Act pathway is a rare concrete example of the complete journey from common law to statute — a rich case for students who need an illustration of how the two sources interact.

nodes.label: Role of parliament in legislating rights
