nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how parliament protects rights through federal and state statute law, and how legislative rights differ from constitutional rights.
criteria: Explains how parliament can legislate to protect rights
Identifies at least one specific piece of legislation and the right it protects
Explains at least one way that statutory rights differ from constitutional rights

width.minimum: Explain how parliament can create, modify or remove statutory rights through legislation, and identify at least one example of a law that protects rights.
width.typical: Explain how parliament protects rights through federal and state statute law, including how legislative rights differ from constitutional protections, and discuss the significance of parliament's capacity to both create and remove statutory rights.
wider: Investigate a case where parliament has legislated to override common law rights or to restrict previously legislated rights, and evaluate the implications
Compare the protections available to First Nations Australians under statute law with those available through constitutional and common law pathways
Examine a state-level statutory bill of rights (e.g. ACT Human Rights Act, Victorian Charter of Human Rights) and evaluate what it can and cannot protect

modes.reason: Including state-level statutory rights instruments (ACT, Victoria) widens students' understanding of how parliament operates at different levels to protect rights — not just federal Parliament.

nodes.label: Comparing and evaluating both institutions' roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the roles of parliament and the High Court in protecting rights, explaining how they interact and evaluating the effectiveness of Australia's overall approach to rights protection.
criteria: Compares parliament and the High Court's roles in rights protection with at least one similarity and one difference
Explains how the two institutions interact (e.g. parliament can respond to court decisions; courts interpret parliamentary legislation)
Offers a supported judgement about the effectiveness of Australia's approach to rights protection

width.minimum: Compare the roles of parliament and the High Court in protecting rights, identifying at least one key similarity and one key difference in how each institution contributes to rights protection.
width.typical: Compare the roles of parliament and the High Court across constitutional, common law, and statute law contexts, explaining how the two institutions interact and evaluating the strengths and limitations of Australia's approach to protecting rights.
wider: Evaluate whether Australia's patchwork approach to rights protection (no national bill of rights; relying on courts, parliament and common law) adequately protects all citizens, including marginalised groups
Analyse the Stolen Generations case and the native title pathway together as a set, drawing conclusions about what each institution can and cannot achieve
Compare Australia's approach with the USA or New Zealand and argue which model better protects citizens' rights, with evidence

modes.reason: Integration node — all earlier content (sources framework, High Court role, parliamentary role) comes together in an evaluative comparison. Teaching investment is in supporting the synthesis and helping students formulate a defensible argument rather than adding new factual content.

descriptors.title: International law and policy
descriptors.description: how Australia's international legal obligations shape Australian law and government policies, including those relating to First Nations Australians, and the issues related to the application of these obligations
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in civic life and contribute to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand the court system's role in applying law (AC9HC9K03, AC9HC9K04).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how Australia's international legal obligations shape Australian law and government policies, including those relating to First Nations Australians, and analyse issues related to applying those obligations.

nodes.label: Australia's key international treaty commitments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the key international treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and explain what signing and ratifying a treaty requires of the Australian Government.
criteria: Identifies at least two international treaties Australia has signed and ratified
Explains the difference between signing and ratifying a treaty
Describes at least one obligation that ratification creates for the Australian Government
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand the signing-ratification-implementation distinction will not be able to analyse the gap between Australia's stated obligations and its actual policies — they lack the conceptual framework to identify issues in application.

width.minimum: Identify at least two international treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and explain the difference between signing and ratifying a treaty.
width.typical: Identify the main categories of international human rights and other treaties Australia has signed and ratified, explain the signing-to-ratification-to-implementation pathway, and describe what these obligations require of the Australian Government.
wider: Research how many of the 9 key UN human rights treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and identify any that Australia has signed but not ratified
Investigate the reservations Australia has entered on certain treaty obligations and what this means for compliance
Examine the role of the UN treaty monitoring bodies and how Australia has engaged with them

modes.reason: The treaty pathway (signed → ratified → implemented) is not self-evident and students frequently conflate stages. Invest in this foundational concept before examining specific treaty effects on domestic law.

nodes.label: How international obligations shape domestic law and policy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how at least one international convention or declaration has shaped Australian law or government policy, using specific examples.
criteria: Identifies at least one international convention or declaration and the obligation it creates
Explains how that obligation has shaped a specific Australian law or government policy
Uses accurate examples with correct names of treaties and policies
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect specific treaties to specific policy changes cannot complete the 'issues in application' analysis that is the descriptor's second key demand — they need the treaty-to-policy link established before they can examine where it breaks down.

width.minimum: Explain how at least one international convention or declaration has shaped a specific Australian law or government policy, using an example.
width.typical: Investigate how international conventions and declarations — including the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, the Paris Agreement, the World Heritage Convention, and the Refugee Convention — have shaped Australian law and government policies, with specific examples for at least two.
wider: Trace in detail how the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples has shaped (or not shaped) Australian government law and policies with respect to First Nations Australians
Analyse Australia's legal obligations under the Paris Agreement (2016) and evaluate the extent to which Australian policy meets those obligations
Investigate how the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and its protocol shape Australia's offshore processing policy, and analyse the issues this creates

modes.reason: Covering at least two distinct treaty-policy examples (e.g. UNDRIP and climate, or climate and refugees) gives students a comparative base — they see that different obligations create different kinds of issues rather than treating all treaties as equivalent.

nodes.label: Issues in applying international obligations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse issues related to Australia's application of its international legal obligations, including tensions between international and domestic law, political will, and enforcement.
criteria: Identifies at least one issue in the application of Australia's international legal obligations
Explains why the issue arises, including at least one factor creating the tension or gap
Connects the analysis to a specific treaty or obligation

width.minimum: Identify at least one issue or tension in Australia's application of an international legal obligation and provide a basic explanation of why the issue arises.
width.typical: Analyse issues related to the application of Australia's international obligations, including: the gap between ratified obligations and domestic implementation, tensions between international law and domestic political interests, and the limits of international enforcement mechanisms.
wider: Evaluate the impact of international obligations on First Nations Australians' reconciliation, truth-telling and sovereignty claims, and assess whether Australia's application of relevant instruments is adequate
Compare cases where Australia has been found non-compliant with international obligations and assess the consequences
Investigate how global interconnectedness both enables more effective compliance with international obligations and creates new areas of obligation

modes.reason: Students need to distinguish between different types of 'issues' — legal uncertainty, political resistance, implementation gaps, and enforcement limits are all different. Structure the analysis to keep these categories clear.
The First Nations reconciliation/sovereignty direction connects international obligations to domestic civic life in a concrete way that makes the abstract enforcement problem tangible.

descriptors.title: Sustaining democracy and cohesion
descriptors.description: the challenges to and ways of sustaining a resilient democracy and a cohesive society in Australia and/or in our region or globally
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in and contribute to civic life in Australia and to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand the influence of media, including social media, in shaping identity and attitudes to diversity (AC9HC9K06).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the challenges to and ways of sustaining a resilient democracy and a cohesive society, examining threats and responses in the Australian and/or global context.

nodes.label: Characteristics of a resilient democracy and cohesive society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies and explain why an active and informed citizenry is important for sustaining them.
criteria: Identifies at least three characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies
Explains why an active and informed citizenry is important for sustaining democracy
Uses accurate civics terminology (e.g. civic participation, social cohesion)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't have a clear model of what a resilient democracy looks like cannot identify what constitutes a threat to it — the threat analysis in the next node requires a baseline understanding of what is being threatened.

width.minimum: Identify at least three key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies and explain why each matters.
width.typical: Explain the key characteristics of cohesive, democratic societies — cooperation, inclusion, respect, peaceful resolution of conflicts, and an active and informed citizenry — and examine how these characteristics reinforce each other.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have articulated the conditions needed for a cohesive and democratic Australia (e.g. through the Uluru Statement from the Heart) and compare with mainstream democratic theory
Explore what 'active citizenship' requires in practice and examine examples of citizens who have strengthened democratic resilience
Examine international research on what makes democracies resilient over time and evaluate how Australia compares

modes.reason: Students often have intuitive but vague notions of democracy. Invest in building a precise, multi-dimensional model before examining threats — the quality of threat analysis depends on how clearly the baseline is defined.

The Uluru Statement direction connects the characteristics of a cohesive democracy to an active civic document produced by First Nations Australians — this is a richer starting point than abstract theory alone.

nodes.label: Threats to democratic resilience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and discuss a range of threats to Australian democracy and democratic societies more broadly, including vested interests, corruption, and the impact of social media on civic debate.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of threat to democratic resilience
Explains how each threat undermines at least one characteristic of a cohesive, democratic society
Uses specific examples or evidence to support the analysis

width.minimum: Identify at least two threats to democratic resilience and explain how each undermines key democratic characteristics.
width.typical: Identify and discuss a range of threats to Australian democracy and other democracies — vested interests, organised crime, corruption and lawlessness, the impact of social media on civic debate quality, extreme polarisation, breakdown of social consensus, and the rise of non-democratic extremist groups — with specific examples.
wider: Investigate how social media disinformation campaigns have affected civic debate quality in Australia and at least one other democracy, comparing the scale and nature of impact
Examine the rise of extremism in a specific democratic context and analyse what conditions allowed non-democratic forces to gain influence
Locate and evaluate data on public trust in democratic institutions in Australia over time and assess what the trends suggest about threats to resilience

modes.reason: The range of threat types is wide and students benefit from encountering examples across multiple categories (social media, corruption, extremism) rather than treating one type as the only threat.

nodes.label: Ways of sustaining democracy and social cohesion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss ways of sustaining democratic resilience and social cohesion, including through public debate, civic participation, and engagement with controversial issues.
criteria: Describes at least two ways of sustaining democratic resilience or social cohesion
Explains how freedom of speech supports participation in public debate
Uses a specific example of a controversial public debate to illustrate the point

width.minimum: Describe at least two ways individuals, groups or institutions can sustain democratic resilience or social cohesion, using a specific example for at least one.
width.typical: Examine how Western democratic heritage and values — including freedom of speech — support participation in public debate about controversial issues, and discuss how citizens and institutions can sustain democratic resilience and social cohesion through specific practices and choices.
wider: Examine a specific controversial public debate (e.g. the date of Australia Day, the Uluru Statement, reconciliation and treaty) and evaluate how the democratic system has handled it — what worked, what failed
Investigate how a non-government organisation or civic movement has worked to sustain social cohesion in Australia, and assess its effectiveness
Explore how countries in the region have responded to threats to democratic resilience and compare their approaches with Australia's

modes.reason: The Australia Day date / Uluru Statement / treaty directions are examples of live, contested public debates where students can examine democratic processes in action — these give the abstract concept of 'sustaining democracy' concrete form.

nodes.label: Evaluating Australia's democratic resilience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate Australia's democratic resilience, considering both threats and responses, and connect this to the responsibilities of active citizenship.
criteria: Makes a supported evaluative claim about Australia's democratic resilience
Identifies at least one significant threat and at least one effective response
Connects the evaluation to the responsibilities of active citizenship

width.minimum: Offer a supported judgement about Australia's democratic resilience, identifying both a significant threat and an effective response.
width.typical: Evaluate Australia's democratic resilience by weighing significant threats against existing responses and mechanisms, and connect this evaluation to what active, informed citizenship requires in the current civic environment.
wider: Evaluate the adequacy of Australia's democratic institutions in addressing reconciliation, truth-telling and First Nations sovereignty, and assess what a more resilient, cohesive democracy would require
Compare Australia's democratic resilience with that of another democracy in the region, drawing evidence-based conclusions
Argue a position on a specific controversial issue (e.g. call for a treaty, Uluru Statement) as an exercise in democratic participation, using evidence and acknowledging opposing views

modes.reason: Integration node — characteristics of democracy, threat analysis, and responses come together in an evaluative argument about Australia's current situation. Teaching investment is in supporting students to move from description to supported evaluation.

descriptors.title: Develop and modify civic questions
descriptors.description: develop and modify questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed and modified questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues at Year 9 (AC9HC9S01). They can formulate sub-questions and revisit questions based on new information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and modify questions that guide sustained civic inquiry, generating productive sub-questions and revising the inquiry based on evidence gathered.

nodes.label: Framing an investigable civic question
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop an overarching inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system or a contemporary civic issue that is specific, investigable, and productively open.
criteria: Develops an overarching inquiry question about a political, legal or civic issue
The question is neither too broad nor a yes/no question — it is genuinely investigable
Can explain what the question is asking and why it matters civically
nodes.hinge_reason: A poorly framed overarching question makes the entire inquiry phase structurally unsound — sub-questions cannot compensate for a question that is too broad, too narrow, or not genuinely investigable. Phase collapse begins here.

width.minimum: Develop one overarching inquiry question about a political, legal or civic issue that is investigable — not too broad, not yes/no.
width.typical: Develop an overarching inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system or a contemporary civic issue that is specific, investigable, and productively open — able to sustain sub-questions and structured inquiry.
wider: Practise framing questions across multiple civic domains (political systems, legal rights, civic participation) and evaluate which framing opens the richest inquiry
Examine examples of civic inquiry questions that led to significant public policy change and analyse what made them productive
Develop and compare overarching questions from the perspectives of different civic actors (e.g. a citizen, an NGO, the government) on the same issue

modes.reason: Teach the criteria for a productive inquiry question explicitly — scope, investigability, openness — before students attempt to frame one. Model the difference between strong and weak framing.

nodes.label: Generating connected sub-questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a range of sub-questions connected to the overarching question that collectively structure a productive investigation.
criteria: Develops at least three sub-questions connected to the overarching question
Sub-questions address different aspects of the investigation (not all asking the same thing)
Can explain how each sub-question contributes to answering the overarching question

width.minimum: Develop at least three sub-questions connected to the overarching question that together cover different aspects of the investigation.
width.typical: Develop a range of sub-questions connected to the overarching question — for example, addressing representation, equality, accountability, and accessibility — and explain how the sub-questions collectively structure the inquiry.
wider: Develop sub-questions that deliberately seek out different perspectives — including those of groups whose voices are less commonly represented in civic debate
Practise generating sub-questions across multiple overarching questions and evaluate which sets of sub-questions best support a structured investigation
Design a full inquiry framework showing how sub-questions connect to different evidence sources

modes.reason: Students often generate sub-questions that are essentially restatements of the main question or that only address one dimension. Scaffold the process of mapping different dimensions of an inquiry (e.g. structural, representational, evaluative) before students generate sub-questions independently.

nodes.label: Revising questions based on evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can revisit and modify their inquiry questions based on further information collected, including identifying whether different groups hold particular views that require the question to be refined.
criteria: Modifies at least one inquiry question in response to evidence collected
Provides a clear explanation of why the modification improves the inquiry
Shows awareness that different groups may hold different views that affect how the question is framed

width.minimum: Modify at least one inquiry question (overarching or sub-question) in response to evidence collected, with an explanation of why the modification improves the inquiry.
width.typical: Revisit the inquiry questions based on further collection of information and modify them to reflect emerging insights — including consideration of whether different groups in society hold particular views on the issue being investigated that require the question framing to be refined.
wider: Trace the evolution of inquiry questions across a complete investigation and reflect on how evidence-driven revision improved the quality of the final inquiry
Practise modifying questions when evidence reveals that the original framing contained an unexamined assumption
Investigate how questions in a real civic inquiry (e.g. a parliamentary inquiry) are modified as submissions and evidence come in

modes.reason: This node integrates questioning skill with the evidence-gathering process — students must hold both the inquiry framework and the emerging evidence in mind simultaneously. Teaching investment is in helping students see modification as a sign of productive inquiry, not failure.

descriptors.title: Locate, select and compare information
descriptors.description: locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students have located, selected and compared information from a range of sources at Year 9 (AC9HC9S02). They can use digital tools to survey political issues and explore media for bias and representation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources about political, legal or civic issues, evaluating sources for credibility, perspective and relevance.

nodes.label: Locating relevant sources across a range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate print and online sources relevant to a political, legal or civic issue, selecting sources that represent varying and conflicting points of view.
criteria: Locates at least three sources relevant to the civic issue
Sources represent at least two different perspectives or points of view
Includes both print/formal and digital sources
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who locate only one perspective or who cannot deliberately seek out conflicting views will produce incomplete analysis — the comparison and evaluation in subsequent nodes depends on having sources that represent genuine variation.

width.minimum: Locate at least three sources on a civic issue that represent at least two different perspectives, including at least one print or formal source and one digital source.
width.typical: Locate print and online sources that represent varying and conflicting points of view on a contemporary political, legal or civic issue, including traditional media, social media, government documents, and survey/polling data.
wider: Use digital survey or polling tools to collect primary data on a political issue and evaluate how survey design affects the results obtained
Investigate how different media environments (traditional vs social media) make particular types of civic information more or less visible or accessible
Locate sources produced by groups whose perspectives are typically underrepresented in mainstream civic debate and evaluate what they add to the issue

modes.reason: Teach source-mapping as a deliberate strategy — students should plan their source search to ensure perspective diversity, not just gather whatever appears first. Model the difference between varied and echo-chamber sourcing.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for credibility and bias
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate sources for credibility, perspective and potential bias, including identifying stereotypes, over-generalisation and misrepresentation in media.
criteria: Evaluates at least two sources for credibility and perspective
Identifies a specific potential bias or limitation in at least one source
Distinguishes between a source's viewpoint and factual error

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two sources for credibility and perspective, identifying one potential bias or limitation in each.
width.typical: Evaluate sources for credibility, perspective and potential bias — including examining traditional and social media texts for stereotypes, over-generalisation and misrepresentation, such as those related to how cultural groups or immigrants are represented.
wider: Conduct a detailed media analysis comparing how two different outlets frame the same civic issue, identifying specific language choices and representation patterns
Investigate how algorithms shape what civic information different users see on social media and evaluate what this means for an informed citizenry
Compare the policies of different political groups on a contested issue and evaluate the framing choices each group makes in presenting their position

modes.reason: Source evaluation requires explicit criteria. Students benefit from a structured framework (e.g. authority, accuracy, purpose, perspective) rather than general scepticism — teach the evaluative categories before applying them to specific sources.

The algorithm and social media direction gives students a systemic rather than individual-source view of bias — understanding how information environments are structured is a different and richer analytical move.

nodes.label: Selecting and comparing across sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select relevant information from multiple sources and compare them to identify patterns, conflicts and gaps in the civic evidence base.
criteria: Selects information from at least three sources
Identifies at least one point of agreement and one point of conflict across sources
Explains what the pattern of agreement and conflict reveals about the issue

width.minimum: Select information from at least three sources and compare them, identifying at least one point of agreement and one point of conflict.
width.typical: Select varying and conflicting information across sources and compare them systematically, identifying points of agreement, conflict and significant gaps — and explaining what these patterns reveal about the civic issue being investigated.
wider: Compare the information available on a civic issue from Australian government sources versus international bodies (e.g. UN reports) and evaluate what each source can and cannot tell you
Investigate a civic issue where survey data and media representation conflict and analyse what explains the difference
Extend source comparison to include perspectives from First Nations Australians or communities directly affected by the issue and evaluate what their perspectives add

modes.reason: This node integrates source location and evaluation into comparative analysis — students must synthesise across multiple sources rather than treating each individually. Teaching investment is in supporting the move from 'source A says X, source B says Y' to 'these sources conflict because...'.

descriptors.title: Analyse civic perspectives and interpretations
descriptors.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have analysed information to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations at Year 9 (AC9HC9S03). They can examine media and information sources for varying views on contemporary issues.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, including assessing the effectiveness of global governance institutions.

nodes.label: Identifying differences in perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different perspectives and interpretations in information about a political, legal or civic issue, explaining what positions different actors hold and why.
criteria: Identifies at least two different perspectives on the issue
Explains why each actor holds their position (not just what it is)
Distinguishes between factual disagreements and value-based disagreements
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can identify positions but cannot explain why different actors hold them are stuck at description — they cannot evaluate the quality or legitimacy of perspectives in the next node without understanding the interests, values and evidence behind each view.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different perspectives on a political, legal or civic issue and explain why each actor holds their position.
width.typical: Examine information from traditional and social media sources to identify different views on and responses to a contemporary Australian political, legal or civic issue — including perspectives from government, advocacy groups, affected communities, and independent commentators.
wider: Examine how the same civic issue is framed differently across media platforms and analyse what the differences reveal about underlying values or interests

Identify perspectives from groups directly affected by a policy (e.g. communities subject to detention policies, First Nations Australians affected by land rights legislation) and compare with official government framing
Investigate how an international body (e.g. UN, ICC) interprets a situation differently from the Australian Government and evaluate what explains the difference

modes.reason: Teach perspective analysis as requiring explanation of motive and interest, not just labelling (e.g. 'Group A supports X because...' not 'Group A supports X'). Model the move from identification to explanation.

nodes.label: Evaluating perspectives and interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, assessing the quality of evidence and reasoning behind each, including identifying value positions.
criteria: Evaluates at least two perspectives, identifying the values positions behind each
Assesses which perspective is better supported by evidence, with reasons
Explains what the differences in interpretation reveal about the underlying civic issue

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two perspectives on an issue, identifying the values positions behind each and offering a supported judgement about which is better supported by evidence.
width.typical: Evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations across sources — assessing the quality of evidence, internal consistency, and the values positions of different actors — and explain what the differences reveal about the civic issue.
wider: Examine the role of global governance institutions (e.g. UN, ICC) and evaluate their effectiveness in upholding democratic norms and human rights, comparing their interpretation with that of the Australian Government

Investigate a contemporary international event — armed conflict, international agreement, humanitarian disaster — and assess the values positions of different global actors (NGOs, governments, the Australian Government)
Evaluate how restrictions on freedoms (movement, trade, association) are justified differently by different actors and assess which justifications best align with democratic values

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to distinguish between their own values and the standards of evidence they are applying. Scaffold this with explicit criteria: What makes an interpretation well-supported? What makes a values position coherent with democratic principles?

The global governance institution direction is a qualitatively different context — evaluating the UN or ICC involves multi-actor international settings where perspectives are structured differently than in domestic civic debate.

nodes.label: Assessing effectiveness of global governance actors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a contemporary international event or situation and assess the effectiveness and values positions of global actors, including the Australian Government's response.
criteria: Identifies at least two global actors and their values positions in relation to a specific international event
Assesses the effectiveness of at least one actor's response with evidence
Evaluates the Australian Government's response to the event

width.minimum: Investigate a contemporary international event or situation and identify the values positions of at least two global actors, including the Australian Government.
width.typical: Investigate a contemporary international event or situation — armed conflict, development of an international agreement, or natural or humanitarian disaster — to assess the effectiveness and values positions of global actors such as NGOs, and evaluate the Australian Government's response.
wider: Compare the responses of at least two different global actors (e.g. an NGO, a government, a multilateral body) to the same event and evaluate which response was most effective and why
Trace how the Australian Government's response to a specific international event has evolved over time and evaluate what drove the changes
Investigate a case where NGO action achieved outcomes that government actors could not and analyse what this reveals about the civic landscape of global governance

modes.reason: Integration node — analysis of global actors, evaluation of perspectives, and assessment of the Australian Government's role are brought together in a specific case study. Teaching investment is in supporting synthesis across the multiple actors and evidence sources.

descriptors.title: Evaluate civic participation methods and outcomes
descriptors.description: evaluate the methods or strategies and outcomes related to making decisions about civic participation
descriptors.knowledge: Students have evaluated the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation at Year 9 (AC9HC9S04). At Year 10 the descriptor adds 'and outcomes' — students are now expected to evaluate not just the method but what the method achieved.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate both the methods or strategies used in civic participation and the outcomes achieved, drawing conclusions about effectiveness and accountability.

nodes.label: Identifying civic participation methods and strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the methods or strategies used by a government, NGO or campaign group to address an issue at regional or global level or to ensure accountability to international obligations.
criteria: Identifies at least two methods or strategies used by a civic actor
Describes what each method involves with sufficient detail to enable evaluation
Connects the method to the specific issue or obligation being addressed
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have a vague understanding of what methods were used cannot evaluate the relationship between method and outcome — knowing that a campaign 'raised awareness' is insufficient for evaluating effectiveness.

width.minimum: Identify and describe at least two methods or strategies used by a civic actor to address a specific issue, with a brief description of what each involves.
width.typical: Examine the methods or strategies used by the Australian Government, a non-government organisation, or a campaigning or pressure group to address an issue at a regional or global level or to ensure accountability to Australia's international obligations — identifying the full range of strategies deployed.
wider: Compare the methods used by a government actor and a non-government actor addressing the same issue and analyse why their strategic choices differ
Investigate how a specific pressure group or advocacy campaign has adapted its methods over time in response to changing political conditions
Research how international accountability mechanisms (e.g. UN treaty review processes) are used as civic participation strategies by NGOs and affected communities

modes.reason: Students benefit from seeing a variety of civic participation methods (lobbying, public campaigns, litigation, international reporting, grassroots organising) before selecting one to evaluate in depth — a thin repertoire produces thin evaluation.

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the methods or strategies and outcomes related to civic participation, making a supported judgement about effectiveness and drawing conclusions about accountability.
criteria: Evaluates at least one civic participation method against its stated or implied aims
Connects method to a specific outcome with supporting evidence
Makes a supported judgement about effectiveness, acknowledging limitations

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one civic participation method, making a supported judgement about its effectiveness by connecting the method to a specific measurable or describable outcome.
width.typical: Evaluate the methods or strategies and outcomes related to civic participation — assessing whether the methods achieved their aims, how effectively they ensured accountability (to international obligations or to affected communities), and what the outcomes reveal about the strengths and limitations of civic participation.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of different civic participation strategies (e.g. litigation vs lobbying vs public campaigning) on the same issue and evaluate which strategy achieved more and why
Evaluate whether a government's or NGO's civic participation methods adequately addressed the needs or rights of First Nations Australians or other affected communities
Investigate a civic participation campaign that failed to achieve its stated outcomes and analyse what factors contributed to the failure

modes.reason: Evaluating civic participation requires students to distinguish between intent and outcome, and between process quality and result quality. Scaffold this distinction explicitly — 'Did the method work?' requires a different kind of evidence than 'Was the method well-designed?'

The campaign failure direction is genuinely different from a success case — analysing failure requires students to identify counterfactual conditions rather than just connecting method to positive outcome.

descriptors.title: Create evidence-based civic arguments
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate evidence
descriptors.knowledge: Students have created descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms at Year 9 (AC9HC9S05). They can construct basic evidence-based arguments.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create well-structured descriptions, explanations and arguments that use civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terminology, with evidence integrated to support claims and conclusions.

nodes.label: Using civics knowledge and terminology accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in written or spoken communication about political, legal or civic issues.
criteria: Uses at least five civics and citizenship terms accurately in context
Demonstrates understanding of terms through appropriate use rather than just definition
Avoids common misuse patterns (e.g. conflating 'law' with 'policy', 'convention' with 'custom')
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who misuse key civics terms produce arguments that are structurally unclear or factually inaccurate — argument quality in subsequent nodes depends on accurate conceptual command. A well-argued position built on a misunderstood concept fails at the foundation.

width.minimum: Use at least five civics and citizenship terms accurately in a description or explanation of a political, legal or civic issue.
width.typical: Use terms and concepts such as 'conventions', 'international law', 'cohesive society', 'global citizen', 'sovereignty', 'ratification', and other relevant civics terminology accurately and appropriately in descriptions and explanations.
wider: Analyse how the same civics term (e.g. 'sovereignty', 'democracy') is used differently in different contexts or by different civic actors, and evaluate what this reveals about the contested nature of civic concepts
Build a personal civics glossary across the unit, tracking how understanding of key terms deepens
Investigate how civic language shapes the way issues are framed in public debate (e.g. 'asylum seeker' vs 'refugee' vs 'illegal immigrant')

modes.reason: Accuracy with civic terminology requires practice and correction. Students who use terms loosely or interchangeably need repeated low-stakes application opportunities before using them in extended argument construction.
The contested language direction (asylum seeker vs refugee) gives students a richer understanding of how terminology is never neutral — this is more than vocabulary practice, it is civic literacy.

nodes.label: Constructing an evidence-based argument
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a structured argument about a civics and citizenship issue that incorporates evidence, draws conclusions, and uses civics knowledge and terminology throughout.
criteria: Constructs an argument with a clear claim supported by at least two pieces of evidence
Uses civics concepts and terminology accurately throughout
Draws a conclusion that follows from the evidence presented

width.minimum: Construct a structured argument about a civics issue that includes a clear claim, at least two pieces of supporting evidence, and a conclusion.
width.typical: Develop an evidence-based argument about a civics and citizenship issue — such as Australia's role in Asia-Pacific security, or trading relationships with nations with human rights issues — that draws on relevant knowledge, uses civics concepts and terms accurately, and draws conclusions about future impacts.
wider: Develop an evidence-based argument that acknowledges and responds to the strongest counter-argument, demonstrating understanding of competing civic perspectives

Construct an argument about a live Australian civic debate (e.g. the Uluru Statement, Australia Day date, treaty with First Nations Australians) that draws on multiple sources and takes a defensible position

Write for a specific audience and purpose — e.g. a submission to a parliamentary inquiry, a letter to a minister, a public opinion piece — evaluating how the argument should be adapted for the context

modes.reason: Argument construction requires students to distinguish claim from evidence, and evidence from assertion. Scaffold the structural logic of argument explicitly — model how evidence connects to claims rather than sitting beside them.

Writing for a specific audience and purpose (parliamentary submission, ministerial letter) gives students a real-world context that sharpens argument construction — purpose shapes what counts as relevant evidence.
